title: Ukraine strikes deep into Russia’s Arctic gas heartland as Trump pushes Putin toward peace
description: Ukrainian drones struck Novy Urengoy, sparking a fire in Russia's top natural-gas region roughly 1,740 miles from Ukraine's border in the Arctic.
fullText:
Ukrainian drones struck deep into Russia's Arctic north Wednesday, sparking a fire at an industrial facility in Novy Urengoy, a city in the heart of Russia's most important natural-gas producing region, according to Russian officials and the Associated Press.

Regional Gov. Dmitry Artyukhov said Russian air defenses repelled the attack but falling drone debris caused a fire at an industrial site. He did not identify the facility, and the extent of the damage was still being assessed, Reuters reported Wednesday.

Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point appeared to claim involvement, posting: "Guess who covered more than 3,300 km and successfully hit the target."

The extraordinary strike comes as Washington makes a renewed push to end the more than four-year war even as Russia and Ukraine intensify long-range attacks on each other.

Ukraine Unleashes More Than 400 Drones Near Moscow In One Of War's Biggest Attacks

Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, President Donald Trump said he had just spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin and suggested both Moscow and Kyiv may be prepared to negotiate.

"We had a great conversation. He is wanting to make a deal. And if Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that would be very nice," Trump said.

Asked what was holding up an agreement, Trump pointed to the personal animosity between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, calling them "two people that hate each other."

"These are two people that are tired of fighting," Trump added.

Trump's comments followed a weekend diplomatic push by U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who traveled to Moscow and Kyiv in an effort to revive negotiations. The talks produced no breakthrough, according to the Associated Press.

Russian Strikes Continue Following Visit By Witkoff And Kushner To Kyiv

Russia resumed major missile and drone attacks on Kyiv shortly after the American delegation left Ukraine, killing five people and wounding 35 on Tuesday, Reuters reported.

A European intelligence source told Fox News Digital that the simultaneous diplomacy and military escalation reflects a long-standing dilemma for Western governments trying to engage Moscow.

"You have to talk, you have to explain," the source said, arguing that communication is necessary to prevent misunderstandings.

Russia Unleashes Nearly 600 Missiles And Drones On Kyiv In Deadliest Strike Since May

But the source said Russian officials can interpret Western outreach differently.

"Whenever you talk with them, they consider that this is a Western weakness," the source said, adding that the assessment was based in part on informal contacts with Russian officials.

The source also said Putin's recent emphasis on Russian "military progress in Ukraine" appeared aimed in part at Washington, projecting strength as U.S. officials seek to revive negotiations.

The escalation is taking an increasing toll on civilians. The United Nations said last month that Russian attacks killed or wounded more Ukrainian civilians in July than in any month since March 2022, with 437 killed and more than 2,600 wounded.

More than 16,800 Ukrainian civilians have been killed and more than 51,000 wounded since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine. Moscow has repeatedly denied deliberately targeting civilians and says its strikes are aimed at military and military-related facilities.

Drone Offensive Hits Russian Oil Tankers And Refineries At 'Industrial Scale' As Moscow Bans Diesel Exports

United24 described Wednesday's attack as the deepest Ukrainian drone strike inside Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Novy Urengoy lies roughly 1,740 miles from Ukraine's border. Artem Zhoga, Putin's envoy to Russia's Urals Federal District, said a Ukrainian drone had attempted to strike a fuel-and-energy facility in Yamal, according to Meduza.

The city sits in Russia's Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, the country's dominant natural-gas producing region. About 80% of Russia's natural gas is extracted there, according to Interfax data cited by the Associated Press.

Artyukhov said there were no reported casualties.

The attack was part of a broader Ukrainian drone assault on Russia. Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces also struck targets around the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, including a naval base, an oil-loading terminal, military port facilities and warships capable of carrying cruise missiles, according to the Associated Press.

Russian authorities said four people, including a child, were killed and 29 wounded in the Novorossiysk attack.

Russia, meanwhile, continued its own long-range campaign against Ukraine Wednesday. Russian drones struck the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, killing two civilians and wounding three, while another wave of attacks on Kyiv killed one person and wounded 14, according to Reuters.

title: Surrogate who refused abortion takes fight to Supreme Court as baby's life hangs in balance
description: Surrogate McKenna West asks the Supreme Court to block a California ruling that left her unable to advocate for a newborn with a rare heart defect.
fullText:
A surrogate who defied a California couple's demand to abort their baby after a devastating heart diagnosis is taking her fight to the U.S. Supreme Court, arguing a lower court ruling has left her powerless to advocate for the medically fragile newborn.

Attorneys for Alaska cardiac nurse McKenna West filed an emergency application Wednesday, asking Justice Elena Kagan to temporarily block a Los Angeles court ruling that declared the California couple the baby's legal parents.

Kagan handles emergency matters arising from the 9th Circuit, which includes California. She has not ruled on the request.

Surrogate Gives Birth In Texas To Baby With Heart Defect After Parents Requested Abortion

West carried the child under a surrogacy agreement with California couple Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed, who call the baby Rumi. West calls him Gabriel.

The baby was born in Texas Aug. 12 with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, or HLHS, a rare condition in which the left side of the heart is severely underdeveloped.

Kagan Recalls Lindsey Graham's Vote That Helped Seal Her Supreme Court Confirmation

The legal war began after the condition was detected during a 20-week ultrasound. West alleges Gilkar and Ahmed asked her to terminate the pregnancy under a provision in their surrogacy agreement covering serious fetal abnormalities.

West refused, telling the surrogacy agency she could not abort "this precious baby" after feeling him move and learning treatment was available, according to the filing.

She offered to raise the child herself or arrange an adoption if the couple no longer wanted him, while allowing them to walk away from any further financial obligations.

Her attorneys allege West was then warned that continuing the pregnancy could expose her to more than $250,000 in financial penalties.

Conservative Groups Say Justice Kagan Cannot Be Impartial In Upcoming Supreme Court Climate Litigation

Gilkar and Ahmed later turned to a California court to establish their legal rights as the baby's parents. West argued the case belonged in Alaska under the surrogacy agreement and said she appeared in California solely to challenge the court's jurisdiction.

The Los Angeles Superior Court determined that West had effectively consented to its authority by submitting a 147-page filing that addressed the "substance of the issues," according to the application.

West's lawyers said most of those pages were exhibits supporting her jurisdictional challenge and that she had repeatedly refused to argue the underlying case.

"Any reasonable view of consent would recognize that 'no' does not mean 'yes,'" they wrote.

West also claims she was never properly served. Her filing says a FedEx package containing the court papers was delivered to her babysitter, who allegedly was not told what was inside.

The California court declared Gilkar and Ahmed the baby's legal parents June 22, and West failed to persuade three state courts to put the ruling on hold.

Surrogate Gives Birth In Texas To Baby With Heart Defect After Parents Requested Abortion

The judge acknowledged during the California proceedings that the dispute "[m]ay be a question of life and death" for the unborn child, according to West's application.

The fight then moved to Texas, where West traveled so the baby could be delivered at a hospital equipped to treat his condition.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton secured an emergency order before the birth, directing the hospital to provide life-saving care and preventing the child from being removed from the state.

West previously said she had only about one minute with the newborn while his umbilical cord was still attached before he was taken from her. A court order later barred her from seeing or holding him.

The baby underwent the first of three anticipated open-heart surgeries Aug. 17. He was later returned to a breathing tube after his condition declined, according to court filings previously reviewed by Fox News Digital.

Gilkar said during a hearing last month in Dallas that the couple had remained at their son's bedside and accused West of trying to take him.

"He's our child," Gilkar said, according to The Associated Press. "He's the love of our lives."

She also told the court the newborn was "suffering a lot" as he struggled to breathe, choked on tubes and required a blood transfusion following surgery, according to the AP.

West has said she would abandon her custody effort if a court determined the intended parents were committed to providing the child with life-saving care.

But on Sept. 2, a Texas judge upheld the California ruling and removed West from the case. Paxton has also stepped away from the legal fight.

Hhs Warns Texas Hospitals Against Denying Life-saving Care To Newborn With Disability

West's attorneys argue she is now barred from receiving information about the baby or defending the order requiring his continued treatment. They allege Gilkar and Ahmed are challenging that medical care order.

The couple previously agreed to the baby's first surgery and said they would approve life-saving care if doctors determined he was a candidate.

West is now asking the Supreme Court to temporarily block the California ruling, which could give her a path back into the Texas case. Her attorneys argue the dispute raises a broader constitutional question over whether challenging a court's authority can itself be treated as accepting that authority.

Her lawyers stressed that temporarily blocking the ruling would not decide who the baby's legal parents are or direct doctors to provide a particular course of treatment. Instead, it could allow West to ask the Texas court to bring her back into the case.

Without Supreme Court intervention, her attorneys warned, West will remain shut out of decisions and updates about the baby's condition as the appeals process plays out.

"Unless this Court provides relief from that judgment, M.W. will have no access to information about Baby G.'s condition," West's attorneys wrote.

They argued that a victory later could come too late to protect the child.

"Relief later in Texas proceedings may only restore her right to protect a child that has already passed," the filing states.

Fox News' Shannon Bream and Bill Mears contributed to this report.

title: Trump, hoping to salvage midterms, makes dubious pledge to give every US adult $5,000 if GOP wins
description: President Donald Trump pledged Wednesday to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, an extraordinary gambit to reverse his part...
fullText:
President Donald Trump pledged Wednesday to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, an extraordinary gambit to reverse his party's sagging fortunes in November.

The dubious promise would likely cost more than $1 trillion and require congressional approval, and would further exacerbate the country's nearly $1.8 trillion annual budget deficit and concerns about inflation.

"If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000," Trump said during the GOP's midterm convention in Dallas. "It will be called the Trump Dividend."

He likened the payments to a corporation's distributions to shareholders, citing "our tremendous strength and success economically."

Within an hour, Vice President JD Vance appeared to try to walk back Trump's proposal — at least in part — by suggesting the dividend payments would not go to the wealthy. Vance suggested it could be paid for by U.S. tariff revenues, though the suggested payment dwarfs what the U.S. has taken in through the protectionist measures.

The White House did not respond to a message seeking details.

Congress would need to approve or otherwise acquiesce to the payment. The sum would far exceed U.S. tariff revenues even before the Supreme Court tossed much of the president's tariff program last year.

The national debt last month topped $40 trillion for the first time.

Trump has frequently lamented that, during the modern era, the president's party almost always loses seats in Congress during the midterms, and he has looked for unorthodox ways to defy the trend, including this week's convention.

"We're going to change that," Trump said. "There's no reason for it."

Marc Goldwein, the senior policy director at the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a think tank in Washington, said Trump has no authority send money to Americans without approval from Congress.

Goldwein added that dividends are something that companies pay when there's a surplus, but the U.S. is running $2 trillion annual deficits and has $40 trillion in debt.

"The idea that we've had fiscal success is backwards and bordering on laughable," he said. "We don't have surpluses to give away."

The move was reminiscent of billionaire Elon Musk's efforts to buy votes in last year's Wisconsin state Supreme Court race, where he handed out million-dollar checks to voters to try to boost a candidate who ultimately lost.

Trump has discussed the possibility before but has never tied it to his party's electoral fortunes. Earlier this year, he proposed a $2,000 dividend and said he didn't think he needed approval from Congress.

Last year, Trump gave members of the military a $1,776 check that he called a "warrior dividend."

"I will get a bill ready so that we can get the Trump Dividend passed immediately after the November 3rd election," Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio wrote on X late Wednesday. "Because Republicans (and America) will win!"

A $5,000 check would give each American more money than they received in direct government payments from COVID-19 relief measures during Trump's first term.

Trump's proposal would be legal because the payment would go to everyone regardless of how they voted, or whether they voted at all, said New Mexico-based attorney John Day.

"This is a campaign promise," Day said. "It's not a payment to individuals to try to get them to vote in a particular way."

Republicans are on defense as they look to defend their narrow House majority against strong headwinds. Trump is unpopular, and Americans overwhelmingly oppose the war in Iran. Even the Senate, which Republicans once were well-positioned to keep, is up for grabs.

title: Wigan prepares to say goodbye to Sir Billy Boston
description: The funeral of rugby league legend Sir Billy Boston will take place in Wigan later.
fullText:
The funeral of rugby league legend Sir Billy Boston will take place later.

Boston, who was the first player in rugby league's 130-year history to receive a knighthood, died last month aged 92.

His funeral will take place at Wigan Warriors' Brick Community Stadium at 12:30 BST, with a limited number of supporters able to attend.

Before the service, a cortege will travel through Wigan , externaland arrive at the stadium. The West Stand will be open as Sir Billy makes his final journey through the Stadium Tunnel. A private burial will follow.

At the request of the Boston family, people attending are being encouraged to wear traditional funeral attire, but items of Wigan Warriors' cherry red can be worn such as scarves, ties and headwear.

People are welcome to pay their respects to the funeral cortege, which will follow a route through Wigan.

Born in Cardiff in 1934, Boston grew up playing union but was overlooked by his home club. He came to the attention of rugby league scouts while on national service in the north of England, signing for Wigan in 1953 as a 19-year-old.

He was picked for the 1954 Great Britain side and was the first black British player to tour Australia and New Zealand.

He reached the 100-try milestone in just 68 matches and claimed 478 tries in 488 games for Wigan, helping them win three Challenge Cups and the Championship.

In all, Boston scored 571 tries in his career - a total surpassed only by Australian legend Brian Bevan in top-class rugby league - and is one of the truly great British rugby league players.

title: Schmidt has an amazing eye for detail - Dermody
description: Ulster forwards coach Clarke Dermody praises Joe Schmidt's "amazing eye for detail" as he settles into his role at the Affidea Stadium.
fullText:
Ulster forwards coach Clarke Dermody has praised Joe Schmidt's "amazing eye for detail" as he settles into his role at the Affidea Stadium.

Former New Zealand prop Dermody arrived from Super Rugby side Highlanders to replace Jimmy Duffy on Richie Murphy's coaching team.

Compatriot and former Ireland head coach Schmidt also arrived at the province this summer to take up the consultancy role of coach development adviser, following a spell as head coach with Australia.

While Schmidt's remit is the development of coaches across the province, Dermody says it is "awesome" to have him around the club as they prepare for the new season.

"A world-renowned coach with an amazing eye for detail," Dermody said of Schmidt when speaking to BBC Sport NI's Nicola McCarthy.

"He looks at the game differently to potentially everyone else. He's not the guy to push that on you, but if you're willing to ask, he's willing to give you that time and not say 'you must do it like this', but he has some ideas around the game.

"To have him around the club is awesome and I know it means a lot to the club for him to come in and spend time working with the youth and the pathways, but around enough for anyone else to rub shoulders with anyone who will want to."

Dermody joked that his main job is to "halve the scrum penalties" Ulster conceded last season, but is happy with what he has seen from the squad so far.

Ulster scored a narrow win over Edinburgh in a pre-season fixture last weekend and will host Ospreys on Friday [19:45 BST] in their final warm-up game before the United Rugby Championship [URC] begins at home to Edinburgh on 25 September.

Although Ulster had a disappointing finish to last season with defeat by Montpellier in the Challenge Cup final and a ninth-place finish in the URC seeing them miss out on the playoffs and a place in the Champions Cup, Dermody feels "the building blocks are there" to push on.

"While it was a tough end to the season, being able to put yourself in a final has to be commended," he added.

"I think there's enough excitement around that to kick-start the season.

"We aren't going to win every game, but there are a lot of games that were close enough to grab a few points that would have made the standing in the table at the end of the season different."

Dermody, who faced Ulster during his playing days with London Irish, recalls an "extremely hard team to beat" and feels getting it right in the forwards is crucial to compliment their attacking play.

"The style of play has changed a wee bit, but I think it would be remiss to overlook the need to express that physicality in the forwards," he continued.

"If you're in most games and the opposition walk off feeling that, you're in a good place."

title: O'Neill 'not sure what to make of' Celtic, so what are the issues?
description: What did manager Martin O'Neill learn about his Celtic squad after a much-changed side earned a narrow 1-0 victory away to St Johnstone?
fullText:
Martin O'Neill was perplexed in Perth.

His "laborious" Celtic side made it six wins out of six in the Scottish Premiership by sneaking by St Johnstone, but his much-changed side far from had it all their own way.

After handing a debut to on-loan Wolves goalkeeper Sam Johnstone, a first Celtic start to midfielder Oliver Sorensen and a rare run-out for centre-back Dane Murray - in addition to recalling winger Sebastian Tounekti and striker Kasper Hogh - the veteran manager would have hoped to have had a better idea of new-looking squad as he "juggles" players and positions.

Speaking after Mika Baur's first goal for the club delivered victory, O'Neill told BBC Sport Scotland "I'm not sure what to make of it, really," while admitting to Sky Sports "we're still well short of it".

With the first Europa League game - at home to Ferencvaros next Thursday - sandwiching a double-header against Rangers, in the Premier Sports Cup on Sunday before the league a week later, it appears O'Neill has some issues to address for a mammoth week.

Watch St Johnstone v Celtic highlights

Despite the tasty triple-header which awaits the reigning champions, O'Neill was insistent on the importance of the match at McDiarmid Park in prioritising their title defence.

It made his fives changes even more surprising. Among them, the omission of Camilo Duran was the most surprising given his blistering start in a Celtic shirt.

Much of the pre-match chat centred on whether the returning Hogh and Duran would play together as strikers or if the Colombian would shift back out wide. No one really considered him being dropped to the bench. And it appears unlikely O'Neill will be tempted to do so again.

"Our main man only came on in the last 10 or 15 minutes, so it gives you food for thought," the Northern Irishman said after his side failed to add to their tally despite upping the ante after Mika Baur's goal early in the second half.

"[Duran's] just been class. He looked tired in the game on Saturday, but I'm not surprised for the amount of things he does for us, both with the ball, which is terrific, and also the work that he does off it.

"He's second only to Daizen Maeda in terms of closing players down. So, I wanted to try and see if we could do without him, and the answer is probably not."

How much will Celtic miss Asian Games-bound Yang?

As delightful as it is to have a diamond like Duran, O'Neill won't want his side to become overly dependent on the 24-year-old in the way they previously did with the now departed Maeda.

Hogh, a poacher, is the polar-opposite to livewire Duran and, with the service as poor as it was from the wings on Wednesday, it was always going to be a night of struggle for the Dane.

He touched the ball just twice in the box before the break, but O'Neill did hint at the club's record signing needing to do more. "You just can't put the ball on a plate for people," he said to Sky Sports. "They have to make room for themselves in the penalty box to try and score a goal."

Yang Hyun-jun was also missed after a glittering start to the season, but the drop-off in confidence, quality and delivery from the South Korea winger to Tounekti was staggering, with former Scotland international James McFadden calling his performance and decision-making "safe" at half-time.

"He likes to come inside, that's pretty positive until the last part," he said on Sky Sports.

"He's got a big problem in his starting position, where he receives the ball, he's always in the eye-line of the defender.

"He's frustrating to watch because he's quick and sharp with good feet, but he's desperate to come inside and never wants to take the risk of going down the outside."

Countless times in the first half especially, Hogh cut an exasperated figure after pulling and pealing away from defenders before not being found by his team-mate.

Celtic lead way from Rangers after narrow wins

The more things change, the more things stay the same. James Forrest starring against St Johnstone.

With 12 to his name, the 35-year-old has scored more goals against the Perth side than any other team in his long and distinguished Celtic career.

He didn't add to that tally but his cameo performance had McFadden calling for the experienced winger to start against Rangers on Sunday.

Forrest flashed a handful of enticing balls across the face of goal, but there were just no takers. He wasn't shy at taking a shot when the opportunity presented itself either.

"I think Forrest starts at the weekend," McFadden added. "He gives you far 

It's an interesting debate with Duran in the conversation too, if he is not deployed through the middle.

On the right, Haissem Hassan's final ball was not much better, but his decision making was more positive as he set up Baur's simple finish.

In principle, yes. In practise, perhaps not yet. In short, Celtic looked like a side who had made five changes.

Yet they faced a St Johnstone team who made four of their own - including a first start for Joe Cotterill - who forced Johnstone into a superb save - and a debut for on-loan Hibs midfielder Josh Campbell.

Pre-match, O'Neill admitted he "had no idea" what midfielder Sorensen was capable of. He may yet still be wondering as the game seemingly passed him by.

It was a bold call to leave Duran and fellow goal-threat Benjamin Nygren - who replaced Sorensen with over 20 minutes to go - on the bench but it did - just - pay off, with the influential pair enjoying a little rest before the Rangers tie.

"I know the results have been fine, really fine, but when we get players up to speed, that'll be great," O'Neill reiterated.

"I think that'll take a few weeks for players. In the meantime, the most important thing is to try and keep your head above water."

title: 'It's NFL everywhere' - American football fever hits Melbourne
description: The LA Rams will face the San Francisco 49ers in the first regular season American football game to be played Down Under.
fullText:
An oval ball, in September, in Melbourne usually means just one thing - the business end of the Australian rules football (AFL) season.

But on Friday, at the unsportingly early time of 7am, 100,000 people will begin filing into the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) for a very un-Australian sporting spectacle - American football.

The LA Rams take on the San Francisco 49ers in their opening National Football League (NFL) fixture, the first time the country has hosted a meaningful, non-exhibition regular season game.

The match sold out months ago, with more than half the crowd expected to be people living outside the state of Victoria. On the official ticket resale site, a restricted view seat is priced at more than A$650 (£350/US$470).

"Walking down the street, it's AFL finals week and you wouldn't even know," says Thomas McMillan, host of the NFL podcast Any Given Sunday Australia.

"It's all NFL everywhere. There are bars that are nothing but 49ers bars or Rams bars. We have a Ram Tram getting around the district. When you're in Melbourne and AFL isn't visible, it shows how big this is at the moment."

Kickoff at 10.35am local time on Friday may not be typical for local fans, but meets the demands of prime time US television schedules and their advertisers.

The league held its first international match in 2007, and over the past two decades the overseas matches have become a long-term strategy to attract supporters and their dollars.

Nine games outside the US are scheduled for the upcoming season, including three in London. But Melbourne is the furthest that players and US-based fans will have to travel.

"Obviously there are question marks when you hear you are playing in Australia," 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey told a press conference this week.

"But it has been so cool… the food's incredible, the coffee's great."

That caffeine reference was perhaps as much to the time zone, as nod to the city's famous café culture.

Melbourne is a mind-warping 17 hours ahead of California where both teams are based, and much of the pre-match attention has been on the two teams and their contrasting approaches to trying to "beat" the jet lag.

For the 49ers, who arrived late last week, their players have had time to get over the long journey, adjust to the time zone, acclimatise and practice at a nearby stadium.

Controversially, the LA Rams are taking things to the other extreme, planning to arrive on Thursday morning local time on a charted Qantas A380 superjumbo, play on Friday, and get back to the US west coast shortly afterwards, in theory to prepare for their next match with minimum disruption to the player's body clocks.

"Definitely it's a gamble," says McMillan. "If they don't quite get things right after the 16-hour flight, you still might have that jet lag, even though you're trying to avoid it."

"And not everyone can sleep on planes," says his co-host Danny Webb. "Whether you're in first class, business class, whatever it is, you're still on a plane."

"And", adds McMillan: "And they're six foot six most of them, so it's going to be even tighter seats".

Despite it technically being a "home" game for the Rams, who bid for NFL marketing rights in Australia under the leagues Global Markets programme, this all means it is the San Francisco 49ers that have more of a presence around Melbourne this week.

And while most practice sessions have been behind closed doors, there have been player appearances at a rally for fans and an AFL match, while ex-stars turned up at that most Australian of traditions, the weekly fundraising "sausage sizzle" at the country's most high-profile hardware chain.

American sports journalist Dontay Atkinson predicts this fan engagement will be reflected inside the stadium and that the MCG will be "heavily red" (the 49ers colour), accusing the Rams of doing "exactly jack squat to sell the NFL brand or connect with Australians".

Writing on X he added: "Fly in, fly out, no contact. I'm sure the Aussies feel great about that snub."

McMillan says he can understand the approach by the Rams, who are seen as contenders for the 2027 Superbowl.

"They're looking at this as a game they need to win," he says.

"We do feel a bit snubbed, and feel the 49ers are doing the right thing,

"But it is their job, so that's where the Rams coaching staff has gone 'nah, we're taking this approach'.

"I just worry that they have missed the boat of ingraining themselves as the Australian team. It leaves it open for others, and the 49ers have really jumped on that."

The LA Rams insist there has been no snub, though speaking to the BBC, the club's Head of International Stephanie Cheng dodged the question of whether she would have preferred her players to have been in town this week.

"It's really a culmination of more than four years of work," she said. "It's not just about game week. We have long term rights."

Cheng says the Rams are the only NFL team with a membership programme for Australian fans, and that it has sent coaches into schools and communities to promote "flag football" – the non-contact version of the sport which will feature in the LA 2028 Olympics.

She also points to regular earlier visits by star players including running back Kyren Williams in March. This week its cheerleaders have visited US military bases in Australia before coming to Melbourne, and the franchise has installed a 22-yard floating football field on Melbourne's Yarra River serving as a fan zone.

"From day one, when we've come to Australia, there's been incredible enthusiasm," Cheng said.

While no Australian players will be on the field on Friday, there are dozens playing US college football and a handful in the NFL.

Most are punters, kicking specialists tapped up after showing their prowess playing AFL or rugby league.

But it is the success of Jordan Mailata, an offensive left tackle with the Philadelphia Eagles, who in 2025 became the first Australian to play in, and win, a Superbowl that was a "major turning point in Australia's fandom of the NFL " says Webb.

"Seeing an Australian in what we'd called a skilled position and then winning a Superbowl. It doesn't get better than that".

Friday's game is the first of three matches in Melbourne to be held over four years, under a contract between the NFL and the state of Victoria.

The league's preference, says Gerrit Meier, managing director and head of NFL International, is to have annual games in Australia similar, to the way the game has grown in the UK.

"We're working off the hypothesis that we need to make a commitment to a market," he told Reuters.

And while many US-based supporters are not fans of the international fixtures, these games are here to stay, says Webb, and the hype and the sell-out crowd in Australia augurs well for it to become a long-term fixture,

"I had mates four years ago asking why are you doing an NFL podcast? It's not a big sport here," he said.

"And now every single one of those mates are asking me for tickets for the game."

title: Zverev storms into semi-finals despite late bedtime
description: Alexander Zverev storms into the US Open last four despite staying up until 3:30am to watch Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz's blockbuster quarter-final.
fullText:
Alexander Zverev booked his place in the US Open semi-finals with a commanding victory over Botic van de Zandschulp - despite staying up until 3:30am to watch Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz's blockbuster quarter-final.

The top seed swept aside the Dutchman with a 6-2 7-5 6-1 win in the night session on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Following his victory, Zverev revealed he had stayed up to watch Shelton's win over defending champion Alcaraz in a match that ended at 03:34 local time on Wednesday - the latest finish in the tournament's history.

"I watched Shelton-Alcaraz until 3.30am last night," Zverev said.

"I did not go to bed, I was up late, I was watching TV because I was sleeping in until 1pm anyway."

The 29-year-old has had plenty of his own late-night finishes at this year's tournament, with his opening three matches ending at 1:55am, 2:15am and 1:09am.

Bidding to reach a third successive Grand Slam final, Zverev will face Russian Karen Khachanov, who advanced after Alexander Blockx retired trailing 6-2 7-5 3-2.

With his win over Van de Zandschulp, Zverev has reached all four Grand Slam semi-finals in a single season for the first time in his career.

"I think the more often that you get to that stage, the more normal it becomes, which is something that you should never take for granted," said Zverev, who ended his wait for a maiden major at this year's French Open.

"I think it's a very special feeling when it becomes normality."

Gauff saves match points to set up Rybakina semi-final

'Just a number' - Rybakina's rise to world number one

Hewett and Reid into last eight of US Open singles

Zverev is the favourite to win the title following Alcaraz's exit, although it has taken time to reach his best level in New York.

The German was taken to five sets in his opening two matches, while he has conceded 80 games at this year's tournament - the second most of any top seed en route to the semi-finals after only Rafael Nadal, who lost 85 games in 2018.

"I think you saw in the first two rounds, I really didn't play well," Zverev said.

"In other tournaments I would be out in the first round, but here I can fight back and play best of five sets, play four-and-a-half hours. I've started playing better throughout the tournament and I'm definitely happy to be in the semi-finals here."

Zverev has won 23 singles matches at majors in 2026 - the most by a German man in a single season, surpassing Boris Becker's 22 in 1989.

Blockx's dream run in New York ended in cruel fashion earlier on Wednesday as the Belgian was forced to retire after suffering a series of injuries in his quarter-final against Khachanov.

Playing in his first Grand Slam quarter-final, the 21-year-old first received medical treatment for a blister on his foot before struggling with a back issue.

"I think today my body just gave up," said Blockx, who had come close to retiring from his fourth-round win against Francisco Cerundolo with a rib injury.

"During the match, it was quite funny to me. I just had to laugh it off because it was just something new the whole time.

"I felt it was getting worse and worse. I couldn't land without feeling pain, without feeling my back, my ribs. So I just didn't want to yeah, maybe make it worse to miss the entire season."

Khachanov wished Blockx a "speedy recovery" after he secured his place in a Grand Slam semi-final for the first time since the Australian Open in 2023.

A former world number eight, a disappointing run of results over the past few months have resulted in Khachanov's ranking dipping to 50 and he is unseeded at a major for the first time since 2018.

The 30-year-old said he will have to come up with his "best form" to defeat Zverev and reach his first major final.

"He's been in the top five for so many years. This year he did also step forward. He won his first Grand Slam, played the final in Wimbledon, as well. He's coming up really in hot form," Khachanov said.

Zverev, meanwhile, says he will have to be wary of his opponent and his extensive knowledge of the game.

"We call him [Khachanov] 'The Professor', actually, because he knows everything about tennis, and he knows every single string tension, knows what everybody does, so that's quite fun," Zverev said.

title: Late goal keeps Rangers on track for Old Firm double-header
description: Rangers celebrated wildly after a stoppage-time strike against St Mirren maintains momentum going into two games with rivals Celtic.
fullText:
If a week is a long time in politics, four minutes can feel like an age in football.

Had Bojan Miovski not rescued Rangers with a neat finish at home to St Mirren as the match entered stoppage time, the post-match talk would have been about the boos ringing round Ibrox.

Hundreds of home fans had already headed for the exits in frustration at a disjointed second-half display.

Instead, after the remaining 270 seconds passed without a St Mirren response, Rangers players and staff flew into the kind of scenes of wild celebrations that normally greet a cup final victory.

Their sails were filled with massive sighs of relief, but where does it really leave Derek McInnes' side heading into two games against city rivals Celtic that could help define their season?

Miovski sparks wild celebrations as Rangers scrape past St Mirren

Rangers winger Yokota suffers 'significant' groin injury

The significance of Miovski's goal cannot be downplayed.

With Celtic beating St Johnstone by the same scoreline in Perth to maintain their own 100% league record, Rangers were so close to falling seven points adrift of the reigning champions only six games into the season.

The wind would have been taken firmly out those sails as they prepare to face Martin O'Neill's men in Sunday's Premier Sports Cup quarter-final before visiting Celtic Park in the Premiership a week later.

As it is, Rangers are now unbeaten in five home games, winning the latest four since losing to Hibernian last month in a game that piled early pressure on McInnes amid his side's exit from European competition.

"If you strip it back, six wins out of seven, four straight wins," the former Heart of Midlothian head coach could rightfully point out. "We have not lost a goal apart from an own goal."

However, since their 5-1 thrashing of holders St Mirren on their last visit to Ibrox a month ago in the League Cup, their four wins have been by a single goal and McInnes recognises that his rebuilt squad are still a work in progress.

"I thought we got what we deserved, granted St Mirren had a 20-minute period in the second half when they were better than us," he told BBC Scotland.

"They played with a bit more belief and came after us and we were guilty of so many poor decisions.

"But I thought the performance for the first hour was really strong, particularly the first half, where we absolutely battered St Mirren.

"I was really pleased with the performance, but at 0-0, as an opposition manager, when you've been put through the ringer and you know you haven't been punished for it, it does give you power and belief that you can get something from it."

McInnes defended the celebrations as understandable in the circumstances.

"Last-minute winners are great for players, coaches and fans," he said. "We'd rather not be in that position, but credit to the players for keeping going.

"There are obviously loads we have to improve on, but we have to meanwhile keep winning and we have to keep improving if we are to achieve anything this season."

Celtic lead way from Rangers after narrow wins

Former Rangers midfielder Andy Halliday believes positive signs are there.

"I thought in the first half Rangers were really good," he told BBC Radio Scotland's Sportsound. "They have shown a vast improvement off the ball over the last three or four games.

"They played with a lot of aggression, a lot of intensity and they've created an abundance of chances in the first half as well, but they just don't seem to have that ruthlessness in the top end of the pitch.

"I don't particularly agree with Derek McInnes' assessment of the second half. I thought St Mirren had much more than a 20-minute period. Rangers just lost all control and got a bit desperate.

"They got a wee bit too forceful too early, but take nothing away from them - the forecefulness worked in the end with the direct ball getting them the goal."

McInnes' ability to find the scoring touch up front has not been helped by long-term injuries to Youssef Chermiti and summer arrival Lawrence Shankland, who started the season as Rangers' first-choice strikers.

The news that Japanese winger Daisuke Yokota will undergo surgery on a groin injury only weeks after his own arrival will add to the frustration.

Having dropped to fifth-choice, Miovski has suddenly emerged as an unlikely saviour.

"It just shows you what football is like and how quickly it can change," Halliday said.

"It looked like he was out of the picture two or three weeks ago and it looked like he was going to be on his way in the transfer window, but he's come up with a massive goal."

While Halliday does not expect Miovski to start next time out against Celtic, he suggested: "He's certainly 

McInnes has so far preferred Ryan Naderi and Kevin Kelsy, the big-money summer arrival from Portland Timbers.

"It is just typical of football that a few weeks ago Bojan would have seemed so far out of it," the manager added.

"But, when you actually strip it back, his goals per minutes in the Premiership is up there with Lawrence Shankland.

"So I was delighted when I inherited someone like Bojan who knows his way about the Scottish Premiership and is a goalscorer and, played in the right manner and with the right partner, is capable of scoring goals."

title: GB's Salisbury & Ram beat champions to reach semis
description: Three-time US Open doubles champions Joe Salisbury and Rajeev Ram beat last year's winners Marcel Granollers and Horacio Zeballos to reach the semi-finals.
fullText:
Reunited three-time US Open men's doubles champions Joe Salisbury and Rajeev Ram knocked out last year's winners Marcel Granollers and Horacio Zeballos to reach the semi-finals.

Britain's Salisbury won the title at at Flushing Meadows in New York alongside American Ram in 2021, 2022 and 2023, but they split in 2024 before teaming up again this year.

They won 6-4 6-4 against the second seeds and will face 2024 runners-up Kevin Krawietz and Tim Putz from Germany on Thursday.

In the other half of the draw, Briton Henry Patten and Finn Harri Heliovaara saved three match points on their way to a 6-7 (7-9) 7-6 (7-3) 6-2 triumph over seventh seeds Manuel Guinard and Guido Andreozzi.

Wimbledon champions and top seeds Patten and Heliovaara spurned four set points in the opening set and had to stave off match points in the second.

They will meet Briton Neal Skupski and American Christian Harrison, who beat Simone Bolelli and Andrea Vavassori 6-3 6-2 in the last quarter-final.

In the women's doubles, top seeds Katerina Siniakova, from the Czech Republic, and American Taylor Townsend are one victory away from lifting all four Grand Slam titles together after winning 6-0 7-6 (10-8) against Diana Shnaider and Elise Mertens.

They will contest Friday's final with Americans Robin Montgomery and Ashlyn Krueger, who saved three match points and came from 8-2 down in the match tie-break to beat second seeds Luisa Stefani and Gabriella Dabrowski 4-6 6-4 7-6 (10-8).

title: Atomic bomb survivor who became baseball legend - Harimoto dies age 86
description: Korean-Japanese baseball legend Isao Harimoto, who survived the atomic bombing of Hiroshima to record the most hits in Japanese baseball history, has died at the age of 86 in Tokyo.
fullText:
Korean-Japanese baseball legend Isao Harimoto, who survived the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, has died in Tokyo at the age of 86.

Harimoto, known as the Hit Machine, recorded the most hits in Japanese baseball history - with 3,085 hits during his 23-season caree. He is the only player in Nippon Professional Baseball League (NPB) history to reach 3,000 hits.

He also hit 504 home runs and stole 319 bases, making him the only player in NPB history with at least 500 homers and 300 stolen bases.

Only three players in Major League Baseball history have achieved the same feat: Barry Bonds, Willie Mays and Alex Rodriguez.

The 18-time all-star player helped the Toei Flyers win their first Japan Series in 1962, and was inducted into the Japanese Baseball Hall of Fame in 1990.

"All members of the Meikyukai express our deep respect and gratitude for Mr Isao Harimoto's many years of great achievements, and we sincerely pray for [following] his passing," the Golden Players Club - one of Japanese baseball's two halls of fame - said in a statement.

Harimoto - whose birth name was Jang Hun - overcame significant obstacles to achieve greatness.

He was born in Hiroshima in 1940 to Korean parents who migrated to Japan during the country's rule of Korea. Though he lived in Japan his entire life and adopted a Japanese name, he did not receive citizenship until later in life.

As a young child, he was involved in an accident that left him with severe burns on his right hand.

With limited mobility in his thumb and forefinger and his middle three fingers frozen into a curled position, he was forced to become a left-handed thrower and hitter.

On his curled right hand, he wore a custom glove that allowed him to catch the ball.

Yet he could have easily never had the opportunity to play baseball.

A year after his accident, Harimoto was in Hiroshima on 6 August, 1945, when the United States detonated an atomic bomb over the city during the final days of World War Two.

The five-year-old survived unharmed - in 2011 he explained that his mother used her body to shield him and his sister after the flash of the bomb exploding. Another sister did not survive.

Harimoto went on to enjoy an outstanding career, joining the Toei Flyers in 1959 with whom he spent 16 years before later representing the Yomiuri Giants and the Lotte Orions.

He won seven batting titles, including four in a row from 1967 to 1970, a feat equalled several decades later by Ichiro Suzuki. He retired in 1981 after playing 2,752 games.

Harimoto helped launch South Korea's KBO baseball league in 1982 before embarking on a career in baseball commentary and punditry.

title: Barca's Rodri apologises over Valencia 'weak' comments
description: Barcelona midfielder Rodri says he has apologised to the entire Valencia squad after television cameras appeared to catch him describing the La Liga strugglers as "very weak".
fullText:
Barcelona midfielder Rodri says he has apologised to the entire Valencia squad after television cameras appeared to catch him describing the La Liga strugglers as "very weak".

Rodri reportedly made the comment to Barcelona team-mates Pau Cubarsi and Raphinha while sitting on the bench after being substituted during his side's 5-0 league win against Valencia on Sunday.

The result at Mestella Stadium left Valencia bottom of the table with no wins in their first four matches.

Though the footage has no audio, broadcaster Movistar claimed they lip-read the 30-year-old former Manchester City player saying: "They're really weak. They haven't got past the halfway line."

Fans and sections of the Spanish media accused Rodri, who won the golden ball as Spain won the 2026 World Cup, of being disrespectful.

"I apologised to my friend and colleague Jose Gaya [Spain defender and Valencia captain] and to the entire squad as well," Rodri said after Barcelona's 5-1 win against Feyenoord in the Champions League on Wednesday.

"I also want to make it clear that it was simply an expression of surprise - anyone watching the video can see that.

"At no point did I intend to mock anyone or take a difficult moment for a team out of context. Quite the opposite - we all want Valencia to return to where it belongs in the league, it is one of the best clubs in the competition. I simply wanted to say that.

"I would also add that it was a private conversation; I think we should all learn a bit more from this, as things really do get taken out of context sometimes. But at no point did I mean any disrespect. My apologies to Valencia."

title: Why is there an NFL game in Australia?
description: The NFL has so far played regular-season games in seven international countries but this week's trip to Australia represents a new frontier for the USA's biggest sports league.
fullText:
The NFL has so far played regular-season games in seven international countries but this week's trip to Australia represents a new frontier.

It is the NFL's first game in the Asia-Pacific region, with the USA's biggest sports league making its longest-ever road trip for the first of a record nine international games in 2026.

It will take place about 10,000 miles from the NFL's New York headquarters, in front of about 100,000 fans at the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground.

That means the Los Angeles Rams will 'host' the San Francisco 49ers on a more open oval field on Friday (01:35 BST).

But when NFL commissioner Roger Goodell visited the MCG for the first time in April, he said the historic arena "speaks to you", and it says "this is the right place to be".

American football is coming to Australia - can it succeed?

Live NFL games have been broadcast in Australia since 1995 and a pre-season exhibition game was held in Sydney in 1999.

Local interest has soared since 2022, though, when the NFL made the global growth of American football a strategic priority.

The league pivoted away from a potential overseas franchise to playing more games internationally. It has invested in new markets before deciding whether to take a game there, holding year-round events to build the fanbase.

Australian players Jordan Mailata (Philadelphia) and Michael Dickson (Seattle) have also captured the imagination down under, playing for the past two Super Bowl winners.

According to the league, the number of fans in Australia has nearly doubled since 2022 to 8.8 million - almost one in three of the country's entire population.

That includes those flooding to one of the world's fastest-growing sports, flag football - the non-contact version of American football.

The NFL played a big part in flag being approved for its Olympic debut at Los Angeles 2028 and has expanded the sport from 10 schools in Australia to more than 500.

Now it aims to help flag football secure a spot at Brisbane 2032, with NFL executive Peter O'Reilly acknowledging that is a key reason for playing in Australia.

Being a sports-mad country, Australia was always on the NFL's radar, and after testing long-distance logistics with trips to Brazil in 2024 and 2025, the league felt ready to head down under.

Sydney and Perth were in the running but Melbourne is regarded as the nation's sports capital and the MCG is the biggest stadium in the southern hemisphere.

A deal was announced in February 2025, during Super Bowl week, and while some fans expressed anger at ticket prices when they went on sale in April 2026, they sold out in minutes.

The state of Victoria is reportedly paying up to A$15m, external (£8m) for the right to host the game but expects one of the state's biggest returns. Dublin enjoyed a tenfold return on its investment to stage its first NFL game last September.

Almost 50% of the MCG tickets were bought by fans outside Victoria or overseas, so about 50,000 fans will visit Melbourne this week.

'The G' is also right next to Melbourne Park, home of tennis' Australian Open, an ideal venue for a three-day fan festival, which began with a watch party for last night's season opener.

The NFL picked this year's Super Bowl week to announce that the 49ers will be the Rams' opponents in Melbourne, which created a buzz in Australia and California.

Not only are the Rams and 49ers regular Super Bowl contenders but they are also divisional rivals in the ultra-competitive NFC West. In addition, there is heaps of hype around the Rams.

With this season's Super Bowl being held in LA, they have gone all-in to reach the big game. First they traded for defensive stars Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie, which cemented them as championship favourites.

Then three-time defensive player of the year Aaron Donald returned from retirement and although the 35-year-old has not travelled to Australia, Garrett and McDuffie will both make their Rams debut at the MCG.

Fred Warner, Nick Bosa and George Kittle are set to return from injury for the 49ers, with Mike Evans making his debut.

The game will be broadcast live on Netflix, reaching more than 200 countries, while the Jonas Brothers will perform a half-time show.

Who will reach Super Bowl? - NFL predictions for 2026 season

California is 17 hours behind Melbourne and the flight takes about 16 hours. The previous longest for a regular-season game was about 12 hours to Sao Paulo, Brazil.

Yet the two teams have taken a completely different approach. The 49ers arrived in Melbourne last Friday while the Rams arrived the day before the game - just as they did for last year's comfortable win at Wembley over the Jacksonville Jaguars.

The huge time difference means that the game kicks off at 10:35 on Friday in Melbourne - which is Thursday evening in the United States: 17:35 on the west coast, 20:35 on the east.

While a morning start (local time) is virtually unheard of in the NFL, it's perfectly normal for fans used to watching cricket at the MCG.

The long flights and early start have thrown each teams' regular routine out of kilter. San Francisco coach Kyle Shanahan admitted he was struggling to remember what day it was.

But having the game in week one gives each team the best chance to cope with the travel demands, rather than playing it later in the season.

Kelce's last dance? Five things to look out for in new NFL season

The NFL has committed to playing one more game in Melbourne in the next three years, with the possibility of another.

What sets Australia apart from other countries hosting international games is that ball-carrying sports are the most popular down under.

All seven Australians in the NFL converted from rugby, basketball or Australian rules football, and Australia has a huge pool of similar athletes with transferable skills.

The NFL has pledged to provide flag football kits to every school in Australia and opened an academy on the Gold Coast as it aims to tap into that talent, which could produce an international pipeline of players targeting the Olympics and the NFL.

title: 'It started as a joke, a fantasy' - F1 heads to football-obsessed Madrid
description: After F1’s explosion in popularity away from its European heartland the sport is coming home. Why Madrid? Because it is beautiful… and has a very big expo centre on the outskirts.
fullText:
You could never accuse Formula 1 of shirking a challenge.

Who else would consider competing for the attention of a football-obsessed country, home to the World Cup winners, in a city where a constant stream of the world's most talented players do awe-inspiring things most weeks?

F1 last had a Spanish world champion 20 years ago and there hasn't been a race in Madrid since 1981.

Does F1, which has experienced a huge rise in popularity in other territories around the world, need another track in its crowded European heartland?

This weekend the sport, and Madrid itself, will find out.

Real Madrid are considered to be the greatest football club in history.

They have won 15 European Cups and 36 La Liga titles, and then there are the famous Galacticos: the generational set of the world's best players which began with the likes of Zinedine Zidane and Ronaldo and has extended to the modern crop that includes Jude Bellingham and Kylian Mbappe.

Some 75,000 Madridistas roared home Mbappe's majestically deft volley to make it 3-0 after half an hour against Malaga at the end of August, and their city rivals Atletico aren't far adrift of them in La Liga. It's hard to see what else the locals need to sate their sporting needs.

But in both the stunning, newly reconditioned steel spaceship of the Bernabeu, which has lost none of the drama of its frighteningly steep theatrical terracing, or Real Madrid women's atmospheric if less salubrious stadium right next to the new F1 track, will fans be turning their attention to the roar of the engine noise this weekend?

"Yes, [the F1 race] is good for Madrid," says one. "There is pride in our sport, Madrid is an open city with open people and open minds.

"The race can [take] Madrid's [identity] outside of football, and the most we can be seen [by the outside world] is the best.

"But I'm more than excited… I'm curious - I want to see how it goes."

"We've always been dreaming of having something [from F1] closer to home," adds another. "Having it back is great. I've been to Barcelona and the Belgian GP and I think let's see how it goes. Organising tends to be messy in the first year - I don't want to be the guinea pig.

"Let's hope it brings the city more into the spotlight. Madrid has a lot to learn from F1 about how to run a global spectacle; F1 could probably learn the true Spanish way. Barcelona is more international, the drivers and fans coming to Madrid will get more of a taste of Spain."

As the Prado museum demonstrates, Madrid knows its fine art.

The crossing signals resemble birdsong and the Mexican conifers gently sway over the waiting traffic with a backdrop of stunning Palaciosian architecture, which is in contrast to the relatively flat, block layout of the inner city.

This may not have made for the best race experience so instead, organisers plumped for what outsiders may see as an unloved expo area run by the quasi-state owned Ifema organisation next to the city's airport.

"It started as a joke, it was a fantasy," says Luis Garcia Abad, Madring boss and former manager to Spain's only world champion Fernando Alonso, among other Spanish sports stars.

"An F1 grand prix is like a unicorn - you are trying always to see the unicorn but at the end you realise [sometimes] it's impossible.

"The queue of cities trying to organise an F1 GP is huge. They have to choose right - we signed a contract for 10 years.

"Maybe seven or eight years ago we talked about this race. At some point Ifema called me and said 'what are you thinking [about its viability]?' After one morning [here] I said: 'It's possible.'

The new venue may be a world away from the flamenco-inspired boutiques and wine bars of the intimate Salamanca district, but Madrid is relatively diminutive compared to other high-profile capitals, and has high-quality public transport.

As a result, organisers are cutting out many of the car parks and asking fans to leave their own motors at home.

But don't expect Patrick Dempsey, Rafael Nadal and Mbappe to be standing on the platform of Avenida de America to hop on the pink line to the circuit – they will breathe easy at the VIP spaces near to the expansive six-strong VIP area paddock.

Regardless of the journey there, what will fans find?

"It's a real experience, not just to be in Madrid but for F1," says Abad. "Every part of the track has its own personality. Monumental… Turn 12, is huge, amazing.

"We really wanted to have an iconic part of the circuit – more than 30,000 people around one corner."

Ah yes, Monumental. The corner everyone in F1 is talking about when discussing this race.

A 26-degree banked challenge, substantially longer than the one at the Dutch Grand Prix's Zandvoort. Monumental scythes through what will feel like a small town come race day.

It comes complete with a VIP viewing area that could house the King of Spain and his family and sits, appropriately, like a castle on top of the hill. The corner itself is a difficult structure to walk up, and in 44C heat, the tarmac is impossible to sit on.

"Luis wanted to think of something recognisable in our circuit. Something iconic," says operations director for Ifema Carlos Jimenez.

Monumental was not the only complex part of a track build, which Jimenez says lends itself to sustainability. Power for the race comes from renewable energy and there is partial use of existing buildings around the site. However, additional construction around the circuit has seen 65m euros of investment, and the track itself cost 85m euros alone.

"There were a lot of challenges," he says. "We started building it in the wettest winter in 20 years in Spain. The rain was torrential. We suffered a lot, and had to stabilise parts of clay which behaves badly with wet conditions. It was very challenging. There are three layers of asphalt here. We learnt from one layer to the next.

"In 2022 it seemed like a little bit of a crazy idea," adds Jimenez. "But Madrid has momentum right now; it's a vibrant city, very well known for football.

"Like a ski resort must have entertainment for apres-ski, a circuit must have good after-race entertainment. Madrid will become in top position - the offer of this city is incredible in terms of gastronomy, a spectacular climate, which is very mild in September. And the party in Madrid is unbeatable."

Make no mistake, Madring is a street circuit: part public roads, part purpose built. And it feels intense to stand on the track, let alone drive it, with the walls on either side appearing to close in on you. And that lack of width, on the eye at least, suggests overtaking will be virtually impossible.

"From a driver's point of view it's quite a harsh circuit," says an excited Abad. "Twenty-two corners, up and down, banking corners - the circuit is adapted to the new [F1] regulations.

"I spoke with Charles Leclerc and he said it was an amazing track, and in the race I believe you will have the opportunity to overtake, but not by free. We're talking about gladiators – the best drivers in the world."

Plenty of drivers have already experienced Madring in anger during a Formula 3 test.

"It's going to be really edgy," says Madrid's own F3 driver Bruno del Pino. "You are always on the limit, the corners are quick and the walls are close. It's like [Saudi GP circuit] Jeddah but with more difficulty.

"With Monumental, you see so much of an angle it never ends. The first time around, you see it going straight up and you feel like you'll fly straight out [of the track].

"It is flat for us because of the downforce so it's not really a corner, but the previous combination of Turns 10 and 11 are high speed and close to the wall - quite a few drivers will kiss the wall."

Britain's F3 driver Freddie Slater goes even further: "A lap of Madrid is so exhilarating, and the adrenaline is pumping - it's an incredible track to drive. It's one of the best tracks on calendar, if not the best.

"It's got character, it's got bumps, uphill and downhill – it's a bit more old-school."

Abad believes it's the spectators who will determine this race's success.

"Not just Madrid needing F1, maybe even F1 needing Madrid," he concludes. "We're investing money to create an experience inside of a city.

"The future of the [F1] championship is something in this direction – we need to take care of customers and spectators. They are our future."

title: Spurs should be awarded 2016-17 title - Pochettino
description: Mauricio Pochettino believes Chelsea should be stripped of the Premier League title for 2016-17, when his Tottenham team finished runners-up.
fullText:
Mauricio Pochettino believes Chelsea should be stripped of the Premier League title for 2016-17, when his Tottenham team finished runners-up.

Chelsea were fined £10.75m in March after being charged by the Premier League for historical breaches of competition rules.

The club also had a six-point deduction "set aside" on appeal. Antonio Conte's Chelsea team finished seven points clear of Pochettino's Spurs in 2016-17.

Chelsea owners Todd Boehly and Clearlake Capital self-reported 74 breaches of Football Association rules when they purchased the club in 2022.

The Blues admitted making £47m in secret payments to unregistered agents and third-parties over transfers between 2011 and 2018.

Pochettino, who managed Spurs from 2014 to 2019, said: "We should win one title, one Premier League. We should have been awarded it.

"[Chelsea] were punished, they admitted, so that's it? The title should be for the team that was second.

"It's true that we didn't compete with the same rules. It's completely fair to say that we didn't compete before the start of the season with the same card."

The current USA coach led Tottenham to the 2019 Champions League final during his five years in charge of Spurs.

They did not win a trophy during his time there, with his best Premier League finish being that second place to Chelsea in 2017.

"Maybe with the same rules, if we apply the same things, maybe we could've signed some players that would have made the team better or scored more goals," added the Argentine, who later became Chelsea boss for the 2023-24 season.

"It's not me complaining - it's the truth. If they admitted they broke the rules, the Premier League title was for the second-best team.

"I'm not scared to say the truth. The Chelsea fans will be upset with me because I'm saying this, but if we were at Tottenham and broke the rules I'd admit the same."

After reporting the potential rule breaches, Chelsea said that it "treated these matters with the utmost seriousness, providing full cooperation to all relevant regulators".

A subsequent investigation by the Premier League found that payments by third parties associated with Chelsea were made to players, unregistered agents and other third parties, which were not disclosed to the regulatory authorities at the time.

The Premier League's report named a number of transfers related to those payments between 2011 and 2018, including those of Eden Hazard, Samuel Eto'o, Willian, Ramires, David Luiz, Andre Schurrle and Nemanja Matic.

There was no suggestion of any wrongdoing on the part of those players. Hazard, Willian, Matic and David Luiz all played for the Blues in 2016-17.

The Premier League assessed a series of recalculations of the club's historical financial submissions, taking into account the previously undisclosed payments, and concluded that Chelsea would not have breached its profitability and sustainability rules had the payments been registered at the time.

It therefore deemed that a points deduction would not be an appropriate punishment.

The £10m fine would have been £20m, but was reduced by 50% on account of Chelsea's proactive self-reporting and co-operation with the process.

The additional £750,000 fine in March was for the registration of academy players between 2019 and 2022, for which Chelsea were also given an immediate nine-month academy transfer ban.

title: Champions Seahawks beat Patriots in season opener
description: Defending champions the Seattle Seahawks come from behind to beat the New England Patriots 13-10 in the opening game of the NFL season.
fullText:
Defending champions the Seattle Seahawks came from behind to beat the New England Patriots 13-10 in the opening game of the NFL season.

For the first time in 10 years the season began with a rematch of the Super Bowl, in which the Patriots were dominated by a Seahawks defence known as 'the Dark Side'.

Again they stepped up after Seattle lost quarterback Sam Darnold to a hip injury in the game's opening drive, claiming three interceptions in the final quarter at Lumen Field.

The Patriots went into a 10-0 lead, with rookie tight end Eli Raridon scoring the first touchdown of the season in the second quarter.

Back-up quarterback Drew Lock got the Seattle offence going late in the third quarter, with Jason Myers cutting the gap with a field goal.

Seahawks cornerback Nehemiah Pritchett claimed his first career interception at the start of the fourth quarter, after a Drake Maye pass was deflected by rookie Rodney Thomas.

On the next possession Lock found wide reciever Jaxon Smith-Njigba in space and last season's offensive player of the year charged through the Patriots defence for a 45-yard touchdown.

Julian Love then picked off Patriots quarterback Maye, giving Myers the chance to edge the Seahawks in front with a 26-yard field goal.

New England were well within field-goal range with 21 seconds remaining, but chose to go for the win rather than settle for overtime, and the move backfired as Maye's hopeful pass towards Mack Hollins was intercepted by Josh Jobe in the endzone.

The only game in which Maye threw multiple interceptions last season was the Super Bowl, and he was picked off on the Patriots' final three possessions in the season opener.

Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel said: "You can't throw three interceptions. Drake knows that."

Maye said his final interception was "unacceptable", adding: "We could have sent it to overtime at the worst, and the only thing I could do was turn the ball over."
