title: O’s lineup finally supports Baz, beat Guardians 9-5
description: One big inning lifted the O’s to a series win over the Guardians
fullText:
A big third inning propelled the Orioles to a convincing 9-5 win over the visiting Guardians on Wednesday night at Camden Yards.

For the second consecutive start, Shane Baz gave up a home run to the second batter of the night. Last time, it was a solo shot from Boston's Mickey Gasper. Tonight, it was a two-run bomb off the bat of Cleveland's Chase DeLauter.

Given how many of Baz's appearances have gone this season, it seemed likely that those two early runs would be enough for the visiting Guardians to win with ease. Coming into this game, Baz had been provided with the least run support of any qualifying starting pitcher in Major League Baseball. Thankfully, for one inning at least, that trend reversed.

Eight of the Orioles nine runs came in the bottom of the third inning. They collected eight hits, walked twice, got hit by a pitch, and benefited from one Guardians error to string together the onslaught.

Leody Taveras and Carlos Narváez led off with back-to-back singles. After a throwing error from pitcher Foster Griffin on a pickoff attempt, Dylan Beavers doubled both of the runners home on a flare that came off the bat at 53.4 mph and landed in the perfect spot beyond the shifted infield and away from any outfielders in the area.

A single for Pete Alonso followed by a Coby Mayo walk loaded the bases before Christian Encarnacion-Strand was hit by a pitch to score Beavers to make a 3-2 game. Jackson Holliday then drove in Alonso on a single into left field for the fourth run of the inning. Rece Hinds nearly left the yard, but had to settle for an RBI sac fly onto the left field warning track to increase the lead to 5-2. From there it was a trio of run-scoring singles from Jeremiah Jackson, Leody Taveras, and Beavers to put a cap on the outburst.

All eight of those runs were charged to Cleveland starter Foster Griffin, who entered the day with impressive season totals. Griffin also faced the Orioles earlier this year as a member of the Washington Nationals. On that June day he tossed seven innings and allowed just one unearned run on three hits, two walks, and nine strikeouts. The outcome was quite different tonight, so kudos to the Orioles for making some improvements in that matchup.

At the same time Baz was cruising on the mound for the O's. From the second inning through the fifth inning, he kept traffic to a minimum, allowing one hit, a walk, and a hit by pitch, but none of them came in the same inning. It felt like the Orioles might be able to coast to the series win.

Of course, that wasn't too be. Baz returned to the mound for the sixth inning, and even retired the first two batters he faced. And then he started to fade. First, he hit Travis Bazzana to put a runner on base. Then, Nathaniel Lowe made him pay with a 407-foot homer that sailed onto the right field flag court to draw the Guardians within four runs.

The scoring didn't stop there, and Baz remained in the game. Angel Genao singled, and then came into score on a Patrick Bailey double that bounced off the base of the right field wall. That was the end of the line for Baz. He was lifted for Josh Walker, who then recorded the third out of the inning without further damage.

Baz didn't have his best stuff in this game. His velocity was down a tick, and there wasn't a ton of swing-and-miss in the Cleveland bats. He was also a bit wild, hitting two batters in addition to his one walk. His 5.2 innings tonight pushed him to 169 frames on the season. That's already more than the 166.1 innings he tossed in all of 2025, so maybe he is showing some fatigue. But the baseball gods owed him a positive outcome tonight. He wasn't great, but his offense finally provided some support.

The Orioles bullpen was quite solid in this one. Walker stayed on the seventh inning after recording the final out of the sixth and kept the Guardians off the board. Yennier Cano was called on the eighth, and he had issues, allowing two base runners and getting just one out. But manager Craig Albernaz didn't allow a meltdown to transpire. He turned to Rico Garcia, who was probably the team's best hurler of the day. He tossed 1.2 shutout innings and struck out three for his seventh save of the season.

Almost all of the Orioles offensive productive was reserved for that third inning, but they did score one 

This was a nice win for the O's. They scored nine runs without Gunnar Henderson, Blaze Alexander, or Samuel Basallo, and largely without extra base hits. Eight of their 10 hits were singles, and the Mayo homer, while nice, was largely inconsequential. Baz was not particularly good, but his bullpen and lineup supported him, which was a nice change of pace for him.

The Blue Jays and Rangers also lost tonight, so the Orioles gained ground on everyone they needed to in the AL wild card race. Their path to a postseason place remains slim, but it does exist.

The O's are off on Thursday before beginning another big series on Friday, this time in Toronto. Chris Bassitt (6-5, 4.96 ERA) will start the opener against his former club. First pitch is set for 7:07 from Rogers Centre.

Here are a few players for your consideration for MBP in tonight's win:

Dylan Beavers (2-for-5, three RBI)

Josh Walker (cleaned up for Baz in the sixth inning)

Rico Garcia (1.2 scoreless innings, got out of Cano's jam)

Shane Baz (finally got some run support)

Coby Mayo (homer off a righty, made the error hurt)

title: First tush push of NFL season draws penalty, spoils would-be drive-saving dart from backup Seahawks QB Drew Lock
description: The infamous tush push appears to continue to be a point of emphasis for NFL officials.
fullText:
With Sam Darnold sidelined, Drew Lock threw what looked like a drive-saving downfield dart for the Seattle Seahawks as they sought their first score of the new NFL season against the New England Patriots Wednesday night.

But a borderline penalty on a failed tush push mitigated the effort, and the Seahawks came away from the drive without any points. The penalty also set the tone for what appears to remain a point of emphasis for NFL officiating.

The sequence started on third-and-22 at Seattle's 33-yard line. With Darnold out of the game with a hip injury sustained on the first drive, Lock dropped back on the third-and-long snap and looked deep dowfield.

He found Jaxon Smith-Njigba just short of the sticks with a laser between multiple Patriots defenders.

Drew Lock and JSN with a big gain on 3rd and 22.

NEvsSEA on NBC/Peacock
Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Bg1bAKodHD

This set up and obvious go-for-it situation on fourth-and-goal near midfield with a 7-0 deficit late in the second quarter.

Go for it, the Seahawks did, with their version of the tush push made infamous by the Philadelphia Eagles. With their iteration, they lined up 251-pound tight end AJ Barner under center in a tight bunch formation. They appeared to get the first down in Patriots territory with a late push on the play.

But a whistle blew. And officials called an offside penalty.

This offside was called on the offense. Officials say right guard Anthony Bradford lined up over the line of scrimmage.

Here's another look. It's tough to tell from NBC's overhead angle if officials got the call right.

Refs flagged the Seahawks offensive line offsides on this successful tush push. Seahawks now forced to punt pic.twitter.com/JjXTrgEsf5

Regardless, the result of the play was a five-yard penalty on Seattle, which resulted in another Seahawks punt, their fourth of the half.

They went into halftime without any points and a 7-0 deficit and Darnold ruled out for the rest of the game.

title: Bullpen Fails as Phillies Slam Astros 11-7
description: It’s only fitting that history was made a mere stone’s throw away from Independence Hall in Philadelphia. Roughly 24,000 players have played Major League Baseball since the N.L. debuted in 1876. Jose Altuve is just the 103rd member to reach the 2,500-hit milestone thanks to a double in the top of third inning.
fullText:
It's only fitting that history was made a mere stone's throw away from Independence Hall in Philadelphia. Roughly 24,000 players have played Major League Baseball since the N.L. debuted in 1876. Jose Altuve is just the 103rd member to reach the 2,500-hit milestone thanks to a double in the top of third inning. Little did he realize that "his moment" would serve as a catalyst for a continued offensive explosion for the night in front of 39,642. Phillies 11 Astros 7.

Throughout the third, the Astros and Phillies would combine to score 8 runs, each posting 4 spots in their respective frames. Isaac Paredes worked some two out magic launching a 2-run blast, his 19th of the year, which brought home Yordan Alvarez. Moments earlier, Alvarez drove in Cam Smith on a double to deep right center. Altuve's historic double preceded a Yainer Diaz singlethat drove him in, making it 4-0.

The Phillies would respond. J.T. Realmuto reached on a leadoff single. Bryan De La Cruz, Trea Turner, Bryce Harper and Luis Arraez joined him with base knocks of their own, and just like that, things were tied up 4-4.

The Astros would regain the lead in the fourth. Cam Smith brought in Daulton Varsho with a 2-run shot to center. For Cam, it was his second straight night with a home run. Sadly. that was where the fun would end for Houston.

Trea Turner sent one to the seats getting one of those runs back in the fifth. Then in the sixth, the wheels officially came off.

Hunter Brown, who was making his 17th start of the year, went five innings. He'd allow 4 runs on 7 hits while striking out 7. Enter Bryan King. Four batters faced, zero retired and to boot a fielding error from Christian Walker. AJ Blubaugh attempted to clean up the mess, but to no avail. Inheriting a bases loaded nightmare, things only went bad to worse. Blubaugh's stuff was missing the corners at an alarming rate. Bryan De La Cruz drew a bases loaded walk which gave Philly the lead, and they'd never relinquish it. At one point, AJ threw a sequence of six straight balls. Kyle Schwarber added the defining exclamation point, clearing the bases with a monster grand slam. It was Schwarber's 44th blast of the season. Philadelphia would score 6 in the 6th, making it 11-6.

In the seventh, Isaac Paredes drove in Houston's 7th run of the night with an RBI single, scoring Jeremy Pena who doubled. Pena now has 30 doubles.

Tatsuya Imai started the bottom half of the seventh issuing back-to-back walks but settled down. Once again in the 8th, Imai allowed multiple base runners to reach but got out unscathed.

The Astros and Phillies would combine for 24 hits on the night.

Kyle Schwarber has now hit 10 career grand slams. Ryan Howard holds their team record with 15.

Cristian Javier will get the start in Thursday's rubber match. First pitch is set for 12:05 CDT. He'll be opposed by Zack Wheeler, who has 12 wins.

title: Barry Melrose Dies: Gretzky-Era L.A. Kings Coach And Longtime ESPN Hockey Analyst Was 70
description: Barry Melrose, who coached the Wayne Gretzky-led Los Angeles Kings team that helped put the NHL and hockey on the map in the U.S., and who later became ESPN’s signature hockey analyst for almost two decades, died Wednesday. He was 70. Melrose retired from ESPN after an almost two-decade broadcasting career after he revealed just …
fullText:
Barry Melrose, who coached the Wayne Gretzky-led Los Angeles Kings team that helped put the NHL and hockey on the map in the U.S., and who later became ESPN's signature hockey analyst for almost two decades, died Wednesday. He was 70.

Melrose retired from ESPN after an almost two-decade broadcasting career after he revealed just before the start of the 2023-24 NHL season that he had been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.

2026 Deaths Photo Gallery: Hollywood & Media Obituaries

Longtime ESPN Hockey Analyst Barry Melrose Retires After Parkinson's Diagnosis

Mark Sanchez Pleads Guilty In Trucker Stabbing Case; Ex-NFL QB & Fox Sports Talking Head Hopes To Avoid Looming Trial & Potential Jail Time

"I've had over 50 extraordinary years playing, coaching and analyzing the world's greatest game, hockey," Melrose said in a statement at the time. "It's now time to hang up my skates and focus on my health, my family, including my supportive wife Cindy, and whatever comes next."

Melrose coached the L.A. Kings the franchise's first Stanley Cup Finals appearance in 1993, Gretzky's fifth season in Los Angeles after arriving in a monumental trade with Edmonton. It was Melrose's first season with the club; he would coach two more seasons in L.A. before turning his attention to TV.

Sporting a mullet, big bright pinstriped suits and with plenty to say, the Saskatchewan-born Melrose became a favorite on ESPN's hockey coverage almost from the beginning when he joined in 1994; the network's coverage of the Stanley Cup playoffs that year won a Sports Emmy. He began a full-time role in October 1996, and he appeared regularly on SportsCenter and NHL studio shows often with ESPNers like Steve Levy and John Buccigross, and also called regular-season and playoff games for ESPN and ABC Sports.

He even parlayed his ESPN fame into other TV roles, playing himself in Mystery Alaska, the 1999 feature about a small-town hockey club playing the NHL's New York Rangers. He also guested as himself in a 2001 episode of ABC's Michael J. Fox sitcom Spin City and appeared in the 2002 sequel Slap Shot 2: Breaking the Ice.

Buccigross remembered Melrose on Wednesday evening,

"Barry was my best friend at ESPN," Buccigross wrote on social media Wednesday night. "A big brother figure of rock solid values. I am shook to my core. Barry gave his life to hockey and some of his ESPN family, like me, learned of his shocking death today while at a hockey rink in Las Vegas preparing for the upcoming season. Chilling and fitting — the rink was Barry's home. A more beloved ESPN institution there has not been. We love you, Barry. Forever."

Barry was my best friend at ESPN. A big brother figure of rock solid values. I am shook to my core. Barry gave his life to hockey and some of his ESPN family, like me, learned of his shocking death today while at a hockey rink in Las Vegas preparing for the upcoming season.… pic.twitter.com/x1zV1b4z87

Said Levy tonight: "For more than 30 years Barry was the unquestioned face/voice of hockey in the United States. He was a man of the people, a family man, a part of my family. Tonight I'll toast the kid from Kelvington who made it big but never forgot his roots. Now he can drink all the Bud Lights, smoke all the cigars and play all the rounds of golf he wants to. Barry Melrose was the best of us."

ESPN hockey voice Steve Levy on the passing of his longtime friend & co-worker Barry Melrose pic.twitter.com/QJ953Q81BC

Melrose played in the NHL as a defenseman with the Winnipeg Jets, Toronto Maple Leafs and Detroit Red Wings from 1979-86. He also played three seasons with Cincinnati in the WHA (1976-79). He later transitioned to coaching, leading teams to Memorial Cup and Calder Cup trophies.

In addition to the Kings, he coached 16 games with the Tampa Bay Lightning in 2008-2009 before returning to ESPN.

title: Multigres v0.1 Alpha: an operating system for Postgres
description: Today we're releasing Multigres v0.1 alpha to the open source community, bringing Vitess-grade horizontal scaling, high availability, and operational simplicity to Postgres.
fullText:
Today we're releasing Multigres v0.1 alpha to the open source community, the first public milestone of our mission to bring Vitess-grade horizontal scaling, high availability, and operational simplicity to Postgres. It's early, it's alpha, and we're excited to get it into your hands.

This is an open-source-only release. Multigres for Supabase is coming soon.

Multigres is a scalable operating system for Postgres: it holistically manages your Postgres instances and gives you sharding, connection pooling, automatic failover, and backup orchestration.

Postgres at scale is operationally complex: You need to manage read replicas, failovers, connection limits, backups, and more. Multigres handles these chores as a single cohesive system. And when the time comes to scale, Multigres will help you shard your database and scale it horizontally.

The v0.1 alpha introduces advanced connection pooling, automatic failovers, and a Kubernetes operator for deployment.

The Kubernetes Multigres Operator allows you to deploy and manage Multigres clusters on Kubernetes. To get started, you need a Kubernetes cluster along with a location for backups configured. The backups can be a shared file system or a cloud storage bucket like AWS S3. It is also possible to run Multigres on a local Kind cluster.

All the necessary images for running Multigres are publicly available.

Multigres treats HA as a consensus problem, and is capable of resolving split-brain scenarios without losing commits that have succeeded. The protocol implemented by Multigres is based on generalized consensus, a model that gives you flexibilities that do not exist in traditional consensus-based systems:

Multigres ships its own connection pooling solution using a two-service architecture. It consists of a multigateway that accepts client connections and routes queries, and a multipooler that manages backend connections. This architecture provides some distinct advantages over a single-process pooler.

Multigres uses pgBackRest for backups. Backups are taken from replicas to avoid overloading the primary.

To learn more about how a cluster bootstraps, you may read How a Multigres Cluster Bootstraps.

v0.1 is stable enough to experiment with and give feedback on. It is not yet ready for production workloads. Specific caveats:

title: The Open Source AI Stack
fullText:
As the quality of open source models have bridged the gap with closed source models, a lot of developers and organizations are looking to move to open source models for more ownership, control and economics. This post is a deep dive into the open model AI stack that developers need to consider as they move from closed to open source.

Using open models for agentic software development does not require learning how to train models, buying a rack full of GPUs, or becoming an expert in machine learning. From the perspective of an application developer, the stack is surprisingly familiar to using closed-source models. You have a model that answers prompts and a harness that manages the interaction between you and that model.

If you already know how to use Claude Code, you’re much closer to using open models than you probably think.

The stack can be broken down into these separate parts:

These layers are all independent from one another, which opens the door for technical decisions at each layer that better suit your development workflow. In turn, this allows you to experiment with new models as soon as they are released.

New models appear constantly. Some are faster. Some are cheaper. Some are unusually good at a particular kind of work. If switching models takes a few minutes instead of rebuilding your workflow, you can actually experiment with them.

In this post we will explore each layer of the stack, explain what it does, and look into how it can be customized. Let’s start with the model layer.

A model takes your prompt and generates a response by predicting the most likely next tokens based on its training data. In our stack, it acts as the intelligence layer and it’s responsible for reasoning, decision-making, and deciding what changes to make in your codebase.

Models come in a range of sizes, and in general, larger models tend to have greater capability, better reasoning, and more reliable performance on complex tasks. Most leading open models are now Mixture-of-Expert (MoE) models that contain many specialized “experts”, but only activate a small subset of them for each token generation. This allows them to have larger parameter counts but only activate a smaller of parameters and thus need less compute to run.

Large models are typically defined by the number of parameters they contain and the amount of compute used to train them. These models have an extraordinary capacity to recognize patterns, relationships, and abstractions from their training data. In practice, “large” usually also implies that the model was trained on more data, for longer, and with significantly more compute resources.

This extra capacity translates into a few important benefits. Large models tend to be better at multi-step reasoning, where they need to keep track of several constraints at once and make decisions that depend on earlier parts of the problem. This makes them excellent choices when given an ambiguous or under-specified task since they can draw on a broader range of learned patterns to fill in missing details.

A good example of a large open model is Kimi K3, which has 1.8T total parameters & 104B active parameters. Reach for large models like Kimi K3 when you need to perform complex tasks, such as:

An advantage of large models is their robustness across different types of work. They can switch between writing code, explaining systems, debugging issues, and planning changes without needing tightly scoped instructions. This makes them especially useful in agent-style workflows where the model has to decide what to do next rather than simply follow a single instruction.

Large models also make better use of longer conversations. When they are given many files, logs, or pieces of information at once, they are able to maintain coherence and connect relevant details across the entire input.

This might lead you to believe that larger models are always better, but in practice there’s a tradeoff between large and small models. Next, we’ll look at some reasons to choose smalls model over larger ones.

The difference between small and large is less about quality and more about how much ambiguity they can comfortably handle.

When a task is clearly defined and tightly scoped, small models can perform on par with much larger ones. If you remove ambiguity by being explicit about what you want, they become extremely effective.

Small models excel at well-specified work since they don’t need to guess your architecture, infer hidden requirements, or explore multiple possible interpretations. They just execute the instruction as given.

An example of a small open model is GLM 5.3 Flash which has 320B total parameters & 18B active parameters. To compare it to Kimi K3, it’s ~6 times smaller and ~20 times cheaper.

These models are surprisingly good when the task is narrow and well-specified, for example:

There is not much ambiguity in these tasks. The model does not need to build a detailed understanding of your entire codebase or decide among several different architecture approaches.

The most important advantage of small models is that they are significantly faster and cheaper to run.

They require less compute to generate each token. In practice this means lower latency responses and a much lower cost per request. For many day-to-day coding tasks, this speed difference is immediately noticeable since the model responds quickly, iterations happen faster, and you can afford to run it repeatedly without worrying about cost.

Rather than thinking of bigger models as being better than smaller models, it’s better to think of these models as two different types of tools in a toolbox.

A larger model might solve a problem more reliably, but it might also be several times slower or more expensive. If a smaller model can make the same one-file change correctly, there is little reason to reach for the larger one.

Over time, start treating model selection more like choosing a tool rather than picking a winner.

Start with a handful of both large and small models, and learn their capabilities and limitations through repeated use. You’ll quickly form an opinion about what tasks in your codebase can be delegated to differently size models.

Next, we'll look at the best places to find models.

New models are released weekly and there are too many models to evaluate all of them yourself.

Leaderboards such as The Open Frontier and Artificial Analysis are useful for discovering what is available and getting a rough sense of how models compare across intelligence, coding ability, speed, and price.

Do not spend too much time trying to identify the single best model on a leaderboard. Benchmarks compress a lot of behavior into one score, while your actual workload is much more specific. A model that ranks slightly lower overall might be excellent at the kind of coding work you do every day.

For reference, the most popular open models in the space right now are GLM 5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Kimi K3, and MiniMax M3. These change very rapidly though.

After you’ve selected a few models to try out, the next step is to find a provider that hosts them.

Because open models are available outside a single ecosystem, you get to choose where they run. The easiest way to get started is with cloud inference providers and cloud gateways.

The way these providers work is that you send them an API request and they run the model on their GPUs. You pay for the input you send to the model and the output from the model, measured in tokens.

This makes cloud providers ideal for experimentation. If you want to try a new model, you can create an API key, specify a model name, and start sending requests. Providers such as Together AI and others offer large catalogs, so a single account can give you access to many different large and small models.

Two providers running the same model should generally produce similar results, especially when you use the same model version and sampling settings. Performance, price, latency, and API features may differ, but the underlying model is still the same.

This separation means that you get to choose a model because you like its behavior, then a provider or gateway based on price or performance.

Models are not uniformly hosted by all inference providers, which unfortunately means you cannot use a single inference provider for every model. Gateways and routers solve this by giving you access to many different models across multiple inference providers. This is especially useful if you want to route between closed and open models.

A gateway sits in front of multiple inference providers and aggregates them behind a single API, letting you route requests across different backends, compare pricing and latency, and switch models without changing your code. It acts as a translation and routing layer between you and the underlying inference providers. Two popular cloud gateways worth exploring are https://openrouter.ai/ and https://vercel.com/ai-gateway.

You can also run your own router locally, or on your own server, with tools like https://www.litellm.ai/. These routers give you a single API endpoint that lets you route between different accounts that you’ve already set up with multiple inference providers.

Once you’ve selected an inference provider or cloud gateway, the next step is to set up your harness.

The harness is the part of the stack you interact with. It’s often a program running on your computer that sits between you, your codebase, and the model. It maintains the conversation and gives the model tools it can use to interact with the real world.

The harness sends that question to the model.

The model might decide the first thing it needs to do to answer that question is search the codebase for terms such as auth, session, or login. It responds by asking the harness to run those searches.

The harness runs the search commands on your computer and sends the results back to the model.

Based on those results, the model asks the harness to read the code from several files. The harness adds the contents of those files to the conversation with the model.

After a few rounds of this, the model has enough information to answer your authentication question. It can answer with all of the files and lines in your codebase that contain auth code.

The important part is that the model is not searching your filesystem or executing shell commands. The model decides what should happen and the harness is the piece that makes it happen.

This means the quality of a coding agent depends on more than just the model.

A good harness knows how to expose tools, collect relevant context, manage long conversations, apply patches, display changes, ask for permission when appropriate, and recover when commands fail.

The same model can feel noticeably different in two different harnesses.

Like models, there is an ever-growing list of harnesses to choose from.

These harnesses come in different forms, including terminal-based CLI harnesses, in-editor extensions that run inside your IDE, and web or desktop applications that provide a more visual interface.

There are also large differences in philosophy.

One harness might expose dozens of features, integrations, background agents, and project management tools. Another might intentionally provide little more than a conversation, a shell, and file editing. Neither approach is inherently better.

Here are a few popular harnesses with support for open models:

Most harnesses make it easy to change from one provider or model to another. In fact, this is often a selling point of open-source harnesses. Switching models is often a single command or configuration change.

For closed-source harnesses like Claude Code and Codex, you can use tools like TogetherLink to connect them to today’s popular open-weight models.

Once you pick a harness, the next step is to customize it for your workflow.

Harnesses can also be extended with skills and MCP servers. These are useful add-ons that provide instructions and tooling that your harness can share with the model.

Skills are reusable instructions that tell a model how to perform a specific task or work with a particular tool. Instead of putting everything into one large prompt, skills can be loaded by the harness when needed, giving the model specialized knowledge for things like deploying an app, reviewing code, or working with a framework. You can discover community skills on the https://www.skills.sh/ website.

MCP, short for Model Context Protocol, is a standard for connecting AI agents to external tools and data sources through a common interface. These servers let a harness interact with things like databases, APIs, file systems, and developer tools without needing a custom integration for each one. You can find existing MCP servers on the https://mcp.so/ website. Different providers also have their own MCP servers. For example, the Together AI one is here.

Next, we’ll explore how to effectively work with context inside your harness.

Once you start switching between models, context becomes important.

Context is everything shared with the model in the current conversation. It includes your prompts, the model’s previous responses, files the harness has attached, shell output, search results, tool calls, and anything else accumulated during the session.

Models have a maximum amount of context they can process. Even before reaching that hard limit, very long conversations can become less useful.

A coding session might start with a narrowly defined task and eventually accumulate twenty files, several failed approaches, pages of test output, and discussions that are no longer relevant.

The model now has to reason through all of that every time it responds.

One of the easiest ways to improve the model’s output is knowing when to stop the current session and start a new conversation.

One of the simplest improvements you can make to an agent workflow is starting new threads more often.

For example, if you finish one task make sure to start a new session before beginning the next task. Or, if you tried one approach and want to reconsider the problem from a different angle, start fresh.

And if you switch models, it is better to start fresh there as well.

This is because the conversation itself influences how the model approaches the problem. A new model dropped into a long debugging session inherits all the assumptions, experiments, and dead ends from the previous session.

One workflow worth experimenting with is to split your prompts across three different models, each with a specific goal. The first model plans, the second model implements, and the third model reviews.

Larger models are excellent planners. They are able to break down open-ended prompts into well-defined and isolated tasks.

From there, use a small model and start implementing each of the tasks one at a time. Create a new session for each task to keep the context small and focused. If any task turns out to be too complicated for the smaller model, switch to a larger model and let it complete the work.

Finally, a large model can review all the work once the tasks are complete. If problems arise during review, this entire process can repeat itself. A new planning session can be created from review feedback causing the whole process to loop back on itself.

One benefit of this approach is that you do not need to turn it into a formal system. Being comfortable using different models allows you to quickly jump between planning, implementing, and reviewing throughout the day as you work in your codebase.

Understanding the layers of the stack allows you to easily experiment with different models, providers, and harnesses without having to change your entire workflow. In most cases, swapping a model is as simple as changing a configuration value. Switching providers is just pointing the same harness at a different API endpoint. Even more structural changes, like introducing a router or gateway, can be added without touching how you actually work day to day.

This separation removes the usual friction that comes with adopting new models. Instead of committing to a single system, you can treat models as interchangeable components in a stable workflow. Your harness stays consistent, your tools and shortcuts remain the same, and only the underlying intelligence layer changes. That makes it easy to test drive models on real tasks, compare cost and latency in practice, and gradually build intuition for which models work best for which kinds of problems.

You can iterate on your stack continuously by upgrading models, switching providers, or adding routing layers, without ever losing momentum in your day-to-day development work.

The most exciting part of open models is not simply that you have more models to choose from. It’s that the entire stack becomes composable.

You can choose a model based on task, a provider/gateway based on your price and performance, a harness based on how you like to work, and extend that harness with whatever skills and tools your workflow needs.

For example, your coding stack could be OpenCode as the harness, GLM 5.3 Flash running on Together AI, the grill-me & hallmark skills for building great UIs, and Playwright MCP for browser automation.

None of these pieces need to come from the same company. And if a better model comes out next week, you can just swap it in without replacing anything else. With open-weight models, you also have the option to take the model elsewhere or even run it yourself (even on your own laptop with tools like ollama).

This is the larger promise of open models.

Instead of choosing an AI coding product, you can build your own AI coding stack.

title: He's Seen Images of 9/11 from Just About Every Angle. Except This One.
description: The 9/11 completist community wants to know and see everything. The Holy Grail? Pictures from inside the twin towers.
fullText:
Michael Wilson reported this story from New York and Indiana.

When he was 15 years old, Jonathan Walczak came upon a newspaper article that described a disposable camera found in the pocket of a dead man in the rubble of the World Trade Center.

An F.B.I. agent quoted in that 2003 article said his team had developed the film from the camera, revealing pictures taken from inside one of the towers as the Sept. 11 attacks were unfolding.

Jonathan had been to the twin towers, once, with his grandparents and his younger brother when he was little. He read to the end of the article, then he read it again and clipped it out. The description of those photos cast a spell on him that he could not shake. An extremely specific fixation took root.

Years passed. Mr. Walczak graduated from college in North Carolina and became a newspaper reporter before moving to Manhattan in 2010 to attend graduate school. He lasted only one semester, but that fall in the city triggered memories. He watched the ninth anniversary of the terror attacks, and thought about that camera. He had kept the newspaper clipping all those years. Where was the camera now? Could he see those pictures? They sounded so vivid.

His time as a reporter taught him how to access government documents. Later that year, Mr. Walczak, now in his early 20s, filed a request under the Freedom of Information Act — his first of many — demanding that the F.B.I. release the pictures from that disposable camera.

“There is no other camera like this,” he wrote in his request. “There are no other photos like these.”

Mr. Walczak is quick to clarify something at this point in conversations about the missing film. He does not believe the pictures will reveal some hidden explanation for the events of that day. He is not a conspiracy theorist.

He is something different — a Sept. 11 completist. The two can look very similar from a distance, people foraging for things that will supposedly show what really happened on that day. But Mr. Walczak has a track record of actually finding them.

On an episode of a 2021 podcast he created, “Missing on 9/11,” he rattled off a list of photos that he has verified were taken on various floors of the towers: “One picture from the 48th, three from the 35th, one from the 51st, five from the 74th, two from the 61st.”

And in his sprawling, labyrinthine quest for those photographs, he would come to know a community of sleuths intent on finding and preserving unseen footage from that singular day. They huddle in Reddit threads, inspecting images and triangulating the exact positions of the photographers.

“People just assume everything’s been published,” Mr. Walczak said. “Not only is that not true, there’s a lot of fascinating footage that hasn’t been published.”

It is like they are working together on a puzzle that, 25 years later, still seems not quite complete. And new pieces keep emerging.

Just this year, amateur Sept. 11 archivists have found a gripping video from a forgotten Camcorder, and another showing office equipment falling from the highest floors — likely thrown through the reinforced glass windows by people desperate for fresh air. These are marked within the community as major discoveries.

But for Mr. Walczak, the disposable camera remains the big one.

The story that the teenage Jonathan Walczak clipped out was written by a Baltimore Sun reporter named Laura Sullivan. In 2003, she spent time with the F.B.I. Explosives Unit at its storage facility in Quantico, Va., a main repository for evidence from Sept. 11.

Deep in the article, her focus turned to the disposable camera. Mr. Walczak has reread those sentences countless times, analyzing them for clues about the photographer or the people around him that day.

“Unit members found a disposable camera in the pocket of a man who jumped from one of the towers,” Ms. Sullivan wrote. “When they developed the film months later, investigators found a chilling chronology of the man’s experience that morning.”

“The photos show the man, who appears to be a construction worker, standing at the window as the other tower burns behind him. The photos, which include pictures he took as well as a few taken by someone else, also capture other jumpers falling. The man looks stricken, his face one of shock and disbelief.”

There were solid clues to chase down. Construction worker … the photo taken as the other tower burns.

The specificity of this description intrigued him. Many articles, books, documentaries and films have been made about that morning in Manhattan. One would imagine that there’s nothing new. But relatively few images from inside the towers have been seen. And none are known to have surfaced from the floors above where the planes hit.

He sought to convey the significance of the photos in his podcast in 2021.

“To me, they’re the Zapruder film of 9/11,” he said. “They’re singular and unique, a point of view unlike any other, documenting a monumental moment in American history.”

But time after time, in his view, he was stonewalled by the F.B.I.

He pursued other avenues. During the “Missing on 9/11” podcast, he made a bonus episode, “The Disposable Camera.” And he invited a guest: the reporter who wrote the Sun story 18 years earlier.

“I email you out of the blue,” Mr. Walczak reminded the reporter, Ms. Sullivan, by then with National Public Radio. “Did you kind of wonder what this is about?”

“I was like, ‘Oh, my God, what did I write?’” she replied. “‘What did I do now?’” But she remembered that day in the Quantico evidence lab.

“I had a flash of Mohamed Atta’s suitcase,” she told Mr. Walczak. “And then it all came rushing back.”

In the evidence room that day in 2003, a brand-new suitcase rested on a table. It belonged to Mr. Atta, a hijacker who struck the north tower — luggage checked so as to avoid drawing suspicion as a passenger with no bags. The suitcase missed the connecting Flight 11 in Boston from Portland, Maine, and thus survived.

She vaguely remembered the photos. Mostly, she remembers the feelings they evoked.

“It was a man in a beige outfit standing by a window,” she told him. “It was sort of the emotional pull of them, that they were taken in this moment of tragedy.”

The pictures seemed to reveal, she said, “this moment that was his last moment — that he didn’t really know it was his last moment.”

Five years after that podcast, Ms. Sullivan can still recall how she felt about the people in the photographs. “Something about them,” she said, “felt trapped.”

She understands the allure of analog found footage.

“In this day and age, we want to be reminded of what’s real,” she said. “An image from that morning of a person living that nightmare, that’s real. And from a disposable camera — it’s real in a way that images today are not.”

As Mr. Walczak dug deeper into the footage from Sept. 11, someone suggested he reach out to a younger man who was regarded as something of an expert. His name was Andrew Boston. Mr. Walczak was skeptical — Mr. Boston was an electrician in his 20s in Nebraska. But he gave him a call.

His doubts vanished: “We spoke for three or four hours.”

Mr. Boston was only 5 years old on Sept. 11, but he remembers it for a specific fright. His father was away on business on the East Coast, and was supposed to fly home that day, but no one had heard from him. His worried mother basically ignored him, and he sat in front of a television showing the scene from Manhattan.

“I do recall the south tower collapse, watching at home,” Mr. Boston says now. “After that my brother and I were sent into the basement, and we played Nintendo. I think my most ever-present thought was, ‘Something very bad is happening.’”

As the afternoon dragged on, the boy ended up on the porch with his mother. Neighbors were outside, too. Then, as Mr. Boston remembers today, there was a tremendous roar overhead. Everyone looked up — it was a huge jet.

“I could see every panel,” Mr. Boston said. A grown-up explained what it was: Air Force One, the president’s plane.

During the chaos that day, Air Force One darted around the country, from Florida to Louisiana to Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska — a few miles from the Boston family’s house.

And a few hours later, Mr. Boston’s father called home — he was safe, his plane diverted to a small airfield.

“It was the first big event of my life,” Mr. Boston, now 30, said. “Every generation has that something that you become aware, ‘Oh, there’s a bigger world than what’s going on around me.’”

To come of age after the attacks is to grow up seeing images from that day. “Wherever you look, documentaries, books — there was always a new thing to learn,” he said.

It followed him into adulthood, where he discovered false claims about what happened that day. “People were, like, just making stuff up,” he said. “This is just bad history.”

Two or three years ago, he began devoting serious time to collecting and cataloging Sept. 11 footage, helping build a community on Reddit called r/911archive. He wanted, for example, to understand — in granular detail — what caused the buildings to collapse. He has sought to understand why some escape routes were available while others were not. He has examined the role of vertical shafts and voids in the collapse.

“It’s a disservice to not try to understand why,” he explained. “It’s history that gets lost.”

The community is still finding footage. Just last year, a newly discovered videocassette — a harrowing scene recorded by a contractor named Edward Sferrazza — was digitized and posted online. It begins with people staring up at one burning building, then a second, and finally, suddenly, everyone is engulfed by ash. Mr. Sferrazza, gasping for air, returns to his van to find two strangers inside, seeking refuge.

“That was huge,” Mr. Boston said of the video. “I’ve never seen something so visceral and so human.”

For his part, Mr. Sferrazza, the contractor, said last week in an interview that he hasn’t watched and has no intention to. He released the video for the sole purpose of rebutting Sept. 11 deniers, he said.

“I just want it to be known that, when they compare it to the moon landing, I was there,” he said. “I smelled it, I tasted it, I lived it.”

Mr. Walczak, though, was not making any progress whatsoever in his search for the disposable rubble camera. Time after time, his Freedom of Information Act requests to the F.B.I. were denied. His description of the material he sought was always too vague, the bureau said.

After having sent more than two dozen requests for documents over 15 years, adding new search terms or names of construction workers who perished, Mr. Walczak finally sued the bureau in federal court last year. He accused the agency of, in effect, not looking hard enough. That lawsuit is playing out in the Southern District of New York, but he felt as if he was nearing a dead end.

There was one more obvious person to contact: the F.B.I. agent who ran the evidence lab in Quantico and who showed the pictures to Ms. Sullivan in 2003.

His name was Donald Sachtleben, and in 2003, he was approaching the end of a remarkable career as a bomb technician — a career that, in the years to follow, would itself implode in spectacular fashion.

His dangerous outings, and the toll they took, are described in detailed court documents.

Mr. Sachtleben, then an agent in his early 30s, gathered evidence in New York after terrorists bombed the World Trade Center in 1993. Impressed with his work, the F.B.I. flew him to Oklahoma City the day Timothy McVeigh detonated a truck bomb at the Federal Building, killing 168. He spent weeks there, picking through corpses for evidence, and after dark, drinking the day’s horrors away in bars.

In 1996, during the Unabomber investigation, agents zeroed in on a suspect: Ted Kaczynski, a recluse who lived in a tiny cabin in the Montana woods. Mr. Sachtleben entered the cabin after Mr. Kaczynski’s arrest, and he found a live bomb under the bed. And it was Mr. Sachtleben — “too stupid to be afraid,” he would say later — who drove the bulldozer carrying the explosives down an icy hill to a spot where the bomb could be safely detonated.

After the attacks of 2001, Mr. Sachtleben worked on the ground in Shanksville, Pa., the scene of the crashed Flight 93. He listened to the black box recording of the passengers wresting control of the plane from the terrorists. “The psychological and emotional toll that work took on Don was enormous,” his lawyers would later state.

He left the F.B.I. in 2008, then returned as a contractor with full access to top secret information. But four years later, investigators made a disturbing discovery when they searched his laptop: He was storing and sharing child sexual abuse imagery. A separate investigation revealed that Mr. Sachtleben had also leaked secret information about a failed bomb plot to the media.

He was arrested and charged in both cases, and pleaded guilty in both. His lawyers said the burnout from his stressful career and heavy drinking led him to use poor judgment. He spent nine years in prison.

During that time, Mr. Walczak tracked him down and wrote to him, asking about the photos from the disposable camera.

Can’t help you, Mr. Sachtleben replied. “There were hundreds of thousands of photos related to the 9/11 investigation,” he wrote from prison. “I imagine these images are tucked away in some storage bin.”

Mr. Sachtleben was released in 2022. Today, he lives far from his old life, in a house at the end of a quiet cul-de-sac near a stocked fishing pond in rural Indiana. Mr. Walczak wrote him here, too, and received the same reply. Can’t help.

When a reporter visited the former agent in August, Mr. Sachtleben listened quietly to questions about the disposable camera and the pictures it yielded.

“I cannot be part of this story,” he said in a brief conversation. He was not allowed to discuss F.B.I. matters without approval, he said.

Asked if he simply remembered the photos, he said: “Somewhat.”

Earlier this year, a head of the F.B.I.’s Record/Information Dissemination Section filed a detailed court response to Mr. Walczak’s lawsuit, outlining the lengths to which the bureau has gone to find this camera. The bureau tried dozens of terms — “disposable,” “rubble,” “camera,” “pocket,” “jumper,” “tower” — in internal search engines, to no avail.

The storage area the Sun reporter had visited is now a mail room, and the evidence that was held there has been transferred elsewhere. Several offices were physically searched in recent months for any sign of the camera or photographs, the F.B.I. said. No luck.

As his search for the camera plods on, Mr. Walczak has become an expert on other so-called rubble cameras found in the ruins of ground zero. Those investigations have proved more fruitful.

He took a deep dive into the contents of a professional-grade camera found at ground zero, and sought to identify its owner by reaching out to the people photographed in the chaotic minutes after the towers were struck. He studied shadows cast by buildings to determine exactly what time different pictures were taken.

He turned that investigation into a documentary called “32 Frames: A 9/11 Mystery.” It arrived on streaming platforms this month.

He gets one question a lot. So does his friend Mr. Boston. So do all the Sept. 11 completists.

“I turned 13 three days before 9/11,” Mr. Walczak said. “It was a coming-of-age moment for me.” The event shook him. And to find community and purpose in revisiting that time after so long — to realize he wasn’t alone in wanting to learn more — is something like a nice surprise.

“These people really deeply care,” he said. “It’s a community of young people who were impacted as kids by 9/11, who the torch has been passed to.”

The attacks immediately sent him back to the day in 2000, visiting the towers with his grandparents as an 11-year-old. I was just there, he thought with wonder on Sept. 11, elevating that day to a core memory. In the same way, Mr. Boston in Nebraska recalls sitting helplessly on his porch, hoping his father was somewhere safe, when the president flew over his house.

Twenty-five years on, they keep coming back to those moments, to that day. Still looking for pieces of a puzzle that the world handed them when they were boys.

title: OpenAI has solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium problem using $15M of AI effort
description: One of the trickiest problems in mathematics has now fallen to AI after just days of work. The groundbreaking result was announced after similar, but less complete work, also created with AI, was announced just hours before
fullText:
OpenAI claims one of its AI models has found a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the toughest and most enduring puzzles in mathematics, sitting on the list of Millennium Prize Problems, solutions for which come with a $1 million reward. The announcement came after an unusual flurry of activity around the problem, along with a dispute around how the work came about.

The Navier-Stokes equations describe how fluids move in space, such as air over an aircraft wing or water out of a tap. Though the equations were first written down around 200 years ago, they aren’t well understood. The question posed by the Clay Mathematics Institute for the Millennium Prize Problem is to determine if the equations always work or if there are situations where they stop making sense and start spouting nonsense, what mathematicians call “blow-ups”.

To settle the question, OpenAI first set 1000 AI agents on the Euler problem, which is a cousin of the Navier-Stokes problem and a step on the path to a full solution. It took the agents 50 hours to find blow-ups in this case. They then set 10,000 agents the task of extending the blow-ups to apply to the full Navier-Stokes problem, which took just 11 hours to finish.

OpenAI said during a press conference that if a customer wanted to run the same problem, it would cost around $15 million. OpenAI didn’t name the AI model used, but said it was “significantly more capable” than even its latest GPT-6 Astra model.

“This problem has remained unsolved for 200 years because the Navier-Stokes equations are just so enormously complex, and the pen-and-paper calculations you need to do in order to solve this problem are just mind-bogglingly intricate,” says Venkat Chandrasekaran at OpenAI, who was also on the press conference call.

Sébastien Bubeck at OpenAI says the news is the “spectacular combination of the arc we have seen over the last 12 months”.

The result is the latest in a string of shocking mathematical discoveries led by AI in recent months. In May, an OpenAI model cracked a decades-old conjecture by Paul Erdős, causing a stir in mathematical circles. Later, the Claude Fable 5 AI found a counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture, which had stood for nearly a century. Last week, an AI model formalised Fermat’s last theorem in just 11 days.

OpenAI’s latest groundbreaking mathematical discovery came just hours after Tristan Buckmaster at New York University and Levent Alpöge at AI company Anthropic announced that they had cracked three significant problems considered “stepping stones” to the Navier-Stokes problem.

Buckmaster and Alpöge also showed that blow-ups can appear in Euler equations; OpenAI has now shown that the same is true of Navier-Stokes.

Buckmaster and Alpöge said they received a “great deal of help from” large language models (LLMs), including LLMs from Anthropic and OpenAI. But when rumours suggested that OpenAI had gone one step further and solved the wider Navier-Stokes puzzle – something the company formally announced just hours later – Buckmaster released a statement suggesting that OpenAI acted unusually and opaquely when he approached the company for clarification.

Buckmaster wrote in a document posted to his website that, as a result of these rumours, he emailed a prominent mathematician at OpenAI to clarify matters. He says that in a subsequent meeting with OpenAI staff, he was given no hard details about how OpenAI achieved the result, but he took what little he was told as a “red flag”, as it appeared to describe the same technique and path that he and Levent had followed to achieve their interim findings.

According to Buckmaster, OpenAI then admitted it hadn’t started its own AI search for a solution until after it had heard of his and Alpöge’s work, and didn’t respond to questions about whether its AI model had been trained or fine-tuned on that existing work – which was being stored in OpenAI’s Codex model, where the company would theoretically have access to it. The pair had used Codex as a customer, not a research partner, so expected that their work should remain secure and private.

Buckmaster makes it clear in his version of events that he is making no claims or accusations about how OpenAI arrived at its solution, saying only that he wished the focus could instead be on the mathematics rather than scandal and intrigue. “I have not seen OpenAI’s proof. I do not know what their model did, or how. I do not know whether our data was used. I am not accusing anyone of anything,” he wrote in the posted document.

In a press conference announcing its discovery, OpenAI categorically denied using Buckmaster and Alpöge’s proof or prompts in its work. It also said that its model’s proof of Euler is different to that put forward by Buckmaster and Alpöge.

It also said that no humans accessed Codex to see work in progress within. Mark Chen at OpenAI, when asked if that also applied to any of the thousands of AI agents that had worked on the problem, said “that’s also our understanding”.

Though the solution to this Navier-Stokes problem has been a long time coming, AI-generated proofs are often hard to understand and rarely bring the same level of new insight than those created by humans. “There’s been this very strange and unprecedented decoupling, this year alone, between getting answers and getting understanding,” says Terence Tao at University of California, Los Angeles. He says that AI is coming up with new results so quickly that there is not enough time for the “slow, deliberate discussion” needed to unpack them.

Something that will happen slowly is determining how the $1 million Millennium Prize money will be awarded. “The process of evaluation is deliberately unhurried, and we shall ensure that it is absolutely rigorous,” wrote Martin Bridson, president of the Clay Mathematics Institute, to New Scientist in an email.

title: America Is the Outlier: What If We Privatized the Airport?
description: America's aviation infrastructure is an outlier. Explore why privatizing airports could unlock the next generation of aerial innovation and growth.
fullText:
Another blue bird day in the Aerial Economy.

A few months back, Nicolas Zart shared with me a statistic that I’m still trying to understand.

America is the outlier in how we own and operate our aviation infrastructure.

The following chart shows the distribution of private participation in airport ownership.

North America checks in at 1% privately owned.

The next generation of aviation is likely to require an uptick in private participation.

Government agencies are not the most efficient systems. We need private funding, the entrepreneurial spirit, and the audacity to create change.

Last night on my drive down Valley, I listened to a podcast on this very topic.

#79 Bob Poole, Reason Foundation: The pros and cons of privatizing airports

Bob Poole parses through the pros and cons of privatization. It’s a must-listen.

And to me - the pros of privatization outweigh the cons. Better rates, more flights, enhanced user experience. It’s not even close.

However, the US Gov is unlikely to relinquish its monopolistic control over our teleportation system.

We love the FAA, but there has to be a better way.

If we’re going to push through the next frontier, aviation may need private motivation.

I’m working through an aerial application for large landowners in the US.

If you build it, they will come.

Message me if you’d like to hear more about how I’m putting the pieces together.

title: Two more men arrested over huge illegal waste dump
description: The site in Kidlington contained about 21,000 tonnes of waste.
fullText:
Two more men have been arrested as part of an ongoing investigation into a giant illegal waste dump.

The site in Kidlington, discovered between the River Cherwell and the A34 in Oxfordshire last October, contained about 21,000 tonnes of waste in a pile 150m (490ft) long and 6m (20ft) high.

The rubbish was cleared during a five-month operation costing an estimated £6m.

A 21-year-old man from Ashford in Surrey and a 43-year-old man from Stanwell in Surrey have been arrested, the Environment Agency (EA) announced.

Previous arrests took place in November, January and February, bringing the total number to six.

Colin Chiverton, area environment manager for the Thames at the EA, said: "The dumping at Kidlington was abhorrent and had no regard for the local community.

"We moved quickly to remove all illegal waste from the site, and our teams continue to work tirelessly on this investigation.

"These arrests are another vital step in collecting new evidence and delivering justice for the residents of Kidlington."

The men have been released on conditional bail pending further investigations.

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle described the arrests as "another step towards delivering justice for Kidlington residents, who have had to put up with the dumping of disgusting waste".

She added: "The years of waste crime being allowed to fester have ended.

"We are taking decisive action through our crackdown and putting more officers on the frontline to restore pride in our communities."

The site, which the EA said was larger than the pitch at Wembley Stadium, was shut down by officers in October 2025. It declared it a critical incident in November.

The agency funded the clear-up, although officials said they would pursue those responsible for the money as their investigation developed.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has set out new plans to shut down the criminal gangs running illegal waste sites, including giving the EA stronger powers to tackle waste crime.

The EA investigation is being led by its National Environmental Crime Unit, with support from Surrey Police and the South East Regional Organised Crime Unit.

title: Prediction markets shift US election odds on small bets, researchers say
description: WASHINGTON, Sept 9 (Reuters) - Prediction markets tracking this year's U.S. congressional elections are "extremely vulnerable" to manipulation as their forecasts can shift on even comparatively small-
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 9 (Reuters) - Prediction markets tracking this year's U.S. congressional elections are "extremely vulnerable" to manipulation as their forecasts can shift on even comparatively small-dollar wagers, ‌according to research published on Wednesday.

The findings from the non-profit research group ‌Anti-Corruption Data Collective are likely to amplify concerns from Democrats and consumer advocates that betting on political races ​jeopardizes public confidence in the electoral system by potentially casting doubt on outcomes or encouraging insider trading.

Representatives for Kalshi and Polymarket, which currently dominate the U.S. prediction market industry, rejected the findings, however, saying Wednesday that market forces created a financial incentive to correct distorted prices ‌by encouraging punters to wager ⁠on the better likelihood.

The booming prediction market industry allows users to bet on the outcomes of virtually anything, including sports, war, drug trials ⁠and elections. Proponents often say the probabilities such markets indicate amount to valuable forecasts, with multiple major media outlets citing market odds in their coverage.

According to the report, for example, ​in more than ​11,000 of the markets tracking congressional races this year ​across Kalshi, Polymarket and Polymarket's U.S. ‌platform, virtually all, or 94%, would see a movement equivalent to 10% in probability following a single bet of less than $1,000. In hundreds of cases on Polymarket, the report said, markets retained their new level for 24 hours and typically did so for around four days.

ACDC researcher Michelle Kendler-Kretsch said political prediction markets attracted large dollar volumes ‌not motivated by short-term profits, which undermined the ​prediction markets' claims to accuracy.

"The conditions for accuracy are ​not being met in markets about ​the November midterms and primaries," she said in a statement.

A Kalshi ‌representative said to the contrary that a ​recent company case ​study showed that, even after a trader had poured more than $1 million into a market concerning former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt, "prices corrected in just nine ​seconds."

A Polymarket spokesperson likewise ‌said that mispriced odds spelled opportunity for other traders: "They are incentivized to get the ​price back to what you would expect it to be."

title: Pilots considered aborting landing after touchdown in Miami cargo crash, NTSB says
description: WASHINGTON, Sept 8 (Reuters) - The National Transportation Safety Board said on Tuesday that evidence recovered from a flight data recorder suggested the pilots considered aborting the landing of an
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 8 (Reuters) - The National Transportation Safety Board said on Tuesday that ‌evidence recovered from a flight data recorder ‌suggested the pilots considered aborting the landing of an ​Amazon Prime Air cargo plane before it crashed in Miami and killed five people on the ground.

The 32-year-old Boeing 767 operated by ‌Miami-based 21 Air ⁠overran the runway by some 1,300 feet (396 m) and crashed into two ⁠vehicles on the ground on Sunday, killing five people and injuring five others.

NTSB Chair Jennifer ​Homendy said ​investigators would interview ​both of the ‌pilots on Wednesday.

The NTSB said that 30 seconds before the end of the flight data recording, the nose landing gear and right main landing gear touched down, while 19 seconds ‌before the end of ​the recording, the left main ​landing gear ​touched down.

A few seconds later, the ‌brakes were released and ​the throttles ​were increased to values consistent with go-around thrust.

The NTSB added there was no indication ​in the ‌recorded data that speed brakes or thrust ​reversers were deployed.

title: Three jurors in Lindsay Clancy's US murder trial point fingers at holdout after mistrial
description: Three jurors from Lindsay Clancy's murder trial expressed frustration during a TV interview that a single holdout juror had prevented them from reaching a
fullText:
BOSTON, Sept 9 (Reuters) - Three jurors from Lindsay Clancy's murder trial expressed frustration during a TV interview that a single holdout juror had prevented them from reaching a verdict of not ‌guilty by reason of insanity for killing her three young children in 2023.

The three women, including the ‌foreperson, spoke publicly for the first time in an interview that aired on Tuesday on the NBC-owned Boston station NBC10. Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, ​Massachusetts, declared a mistrial on Friday after the 12 jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict.

Jurors had repeatedly said they were deadlocked. Foreperson Roni Carlson blamed the impasse on one juror, a man, who refused to change his position despite acknowledging having reasonable doubt.

"He admitted he had reasonable doubt and I started filling out the forms, I was so excited," Carlson ‌said.

But she said the man then ⁠said: "I'm still not going to say that she's not guilty by reason of insanity."

Another juror, Paula Devlin, called the unnamed holdout juror "very arrogant."

"He really did not take anything that anybody said," ⁠she said.

The holdout juror could not be reached for comment, and the names of the jurors are sealed.

DEFENSE ARGUED CLANCY HAD PSYCHOTIC EPISODE

Clancy, 36, has admitted to strangling her three children with exercise bands on January 24, 2023, in the basement of their ​home in ​the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with ​a knife and jumped from a second-story window ‌in an attempt to end her own life that left her paralyzed.

During the six-week trial, defense attorney Kevin Reddington sought to convince jurors she should be found not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility. He argued she was a loving mother who had been in the midst of a psychotic episode when she killed Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan.

Carlson said the jurors were not trying to figure out if she ‌killed the children.

"She did," Carlson said. "And she's admitting that. We're trying ​to figure out, did she know right from wrong at that time? ​And with everybody saying she loved her children ​so much and everything proved she loved her children, from her journals to (testimony by) her ‌mother-in-law. Everything proved that she loved her children, so ​she had to have snapped."

Prosecutors ​have not said if they plan to retry the case. Clancy faces a life sentence without parole if she is eventually convicted of first-degree murder.

"I just found it to be harsh," juror Kellie Farina said ​of the prosecution. "Very, very harsh."

If found not ‌guilty by reason of insanity, Clancy would be committed to a state psychiatric hospital for evaluation. Her ​commitment would then be subject to regular review by the court.

Clancy remains in custody at a ​state hospital.

title: Americans are losing faith in capitalism. The problem isn’t capitalism
description: The public seems to think that shareholder value is a loss for consumers. A Yale research project with over 200 CEO interviews reveals something else.
fullText:
Gallup tracking data shows that positive views of capitalism have slipped to 54%, marking a 15-year low since they began tracking the metric. The finding reflects a zero-sum view of the corporation: that companies prosper by extracting value rather than creating it.

It is no surprise that the more than 200 CEOs we have interviewed over six years through Yale's Program on Stakeholder Innovation and Management reject this zero-sum view. Their reasons, however, may not be what most people assume. They see creating value for customers, employees, partners and communities not as an alternative to shareholder value, but as essential to creating it over the long term.

How did Walmart redesign its business model?

Why are positive views of capitalism declining?

What changes did Starbucks make under Brian Niccol?

How do companies manage intangible value sources?

What may also be surprising is that many told us this was the discipline for which they felt least prepared before becoming CEOs. They understand the importance of the "and"—that these interests can reinforce rather than compete with one another—but struggle with how to make that happen at scale. The problem isn't ideology. It's know-how. Three examples show what that know-how looks like in practice.

When Doug McMillon became Walmart's CEO in 2014, U.S. comparable-store sales were in  decline, customer satisfaction had deteriorated, and the company was losing ground to Amazon.  Employee turnover was high. Walmart's reputation as an employer was turning away some  potential customers and contributing to community resistance to new stores. Its shares had made  little progress for years.

McMillon and his team concluded that Walmart's problems were connected, so the response had to be, too. E-commerce would draw on its strength in grocery and its store network, which required stores customers wanted to visit and engaged, capable employees. Technology would support omnichannel commerce while improving forecasting, inventory and store operations. Productivity and closer supplier coordination would help sustain the lower prices on which customer trust depended.

That approach required billions of dollars of multi-year investments in employees, lower prices,  e-commerce and technology, sacrificing near-term profits. When Walmart disclosed in 2015 how  much these investments would depress earnings, its shares fell about 10% in a single day, wiping  out more than $20 billion in market value.

Despite the market backlash, McMillon and his team stayed the course—and the payoff proved substantial. In February 2026, Walmart became the first traditional retailer to exceed $1 trillion in market value. Comparable-store sales, which had been falling, recovered and then compounded. In 2024, Walmart appeared for the first time on Fortune's list of the 100 Best Companies to Work For.

title: Bank of America exec killed in random Times Square stabbing laid to rest as hundreds mourn young mom
description: The Bank of America VP killed in the Times Square stabbing had just returned from maternity leave. A GoFundMe for her baby nears $1 million.
fullText:
MENDHAM BOROUGH, N.J. — The Bank of America executive killed in a random, unprovoked stabbing in New York City's Times Square last week was laid to rest Wednesday as hundreds of mourners turned out to pay their respects over the past two days.

Erin Guiltinan Piacenti, 32, of Chester, New Jersey, had just returned from maternity leave after the birth of her first child when police say a woman with a history of mental illness stabbed her and another bystander on Seventh Avenue.

Piacenti, the oldest of five siblings, graduated from the University of Pennsylvania and Fordham University School of Law, according to her family's death announcement.

Nj Mom Fatally Stabbed In Times Square During First Week Back At Bank Of America After Maternity Leave

She became the music director of UPenn's Dischord A Cappella group and met her husband, Frank Piacenti, at law school, according to the obituary. The two married in 2024 and welcomed their first and only child, Madison, in March.

After graduation, she worked at the Manhattan-based international law firm of Davis Polk & Wardwell before becoming a vice president at Bank of America.

Piacenti and her husband had returned from a vacation celebrating their two-year anniversary the day before her murder, according to the family.

Aug. 31 was also her first day back from maternity leave, according to the organizer of a GoFundMe campaign that has raised nearly $1 million as of Tuesday for 6-month-old Madison.

Multiple People Stabbed Near Penn Station, Leaving One Seriously Injured As Investigation Continues

At a wake Tuesday evening, hundreds of mourners lined up outside the St. Joseph Catholic Church in Mendham Borough, New Jersey. They came and left in small groups between 3 p.m. and 8 p.m. The church's parking lot full much of the evening, and local police were coordinating traffic.

A funeral Mass was held Wednesday at 11 a.m. ET at the same church.

The family is asking for donations to the GoFundMe in lieu of flowers.

Just before 4:30 p.m. Aug. 31, Piacenti was stabbed in the abdomen in New York's Times Square, according to NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch. The injury proved fatal.

Speaking with reporters on the evening of the murder, Tisch identified the suspect as 49-year-old Queens resident Pamela Cisneros.

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

Just 20 seconds before the attack on Piacenti, Cisneros stabbed a 68-year-old man who was waiting at a crosswalk with his wife, Tisch said, calling the stabbings "random and unprovoked." He survived and was hospitalized in stable condition, according to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Nyc Suspect Freed From Psych Hold Hours Before Fatal Subway Shoving Of 76-Year-old Former Teacher

"I ask New Yorkers to join me in holding the victim in our thoughts and wishing them a full recovery," he said at a news briefing. "I want to thank the NYPD officers who stepped in and prevented a horrific attack from becoming even worse."

A routine investigation into the officers' conduct would be conducted, he said, and the city will release bodycam footage.

Part of a subsequent standoff with police was captured on video. The woman identified as Cisneros can be seen holding two kitchen knives. Police told her repeatedly to drop the weapons.

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

"I'm not dropping anything," she told the officers, according to Tisch. "I would rather kill both of you. I will kill you."

NYPD officers attempted to stop her with stun guns, which failed to stop her. As she approached officers while waving the knives, they opened fire.

The incident caused road closures on Seventh Avenue between 42nd and 47th streets.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Cisneros was pronounced dead at Bellevue Hospital. Tisch said Cisneros had a documented history of mental health issues that led to interactions with the NYPD in 2018 and 2019 but no prior arrests.

"Tonight, our thoughts are, of course, with the victims of this horrific attack and their families," Tisch told reporters near the scene last week. "One life cut far too short by a senseless act of violence."

Fox News' Greg Wehner contributed to this report.
