title: Drone alert delayed Zelenskiy's departure for Norway, Moldova says
description: OSLO, Sept 9 (Reuters) - The plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy to Oslo for the funeral of the king of Norway was nearly struck by a drone when taking off from Moldova on Tuesday,
fullText:
OSLO, Sept 9 (Reuters) - The plane carrying Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy to Oslo for the funeral of the king of Norway ‌was nearly struck by a drone when taking off from Moldova ‌on Tuesday, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere told public broadcaster NRK on Wednesday.

"His plane ​was almost hit by a drone as it was about to take off from Moldova. That is the reality he is facing," said Stoere, who did not say what his source was for the information or how ‌close the drone came.

Officials in ⁠Moldova made no comment on Stoere's statement regarding Zelenskiy's plane.

Arrivals and departures at Chisinau airport were suspended for a ⁠time on Tuesday in connection with two Russian drones that entered Moldovan airspace. Several flights bound for the capital landed at airports outside Moldova or were forced ​into ​holding patterns, according to data from Flightradar24.

One ​drone landed in a field, ‌triggering a fire, while the second carried on into Romanian airspace.

Moldovan President Maia Sandu denounced the intrusions as a "serious threat to people's lives" and also condemned an attack on a border crossing with Ukraine that killed two people.

Zelenskiy attended the funeral of King Harald V of Norway on Wednesday, ‌marching behind his coffin along with other ​heads of state in central Oslo. He ​left Norway soon after the ​funeral was over.

Stoere had said in a statement on ‌Tuesday that he would meet the ​Ukrainian leader that evening, ​with their discussions to focus on Ukraine's air defence.

Zelenskiy had said there would also be discussions with companies taking part in the ​Freyja initiative to create ‌a European anti-ballistic system while he was in Norway.

title: Lady Joan's death linked to lack of medication
description: Lady Joan Branson died after suffering a cardiac arrest at the private Lister Hospital in Chelsea last year.
fullText:
A private hospital's failure to provide preventative medication contributed to the death of Lady Joan Branson, an inquest has concluded.

The 80-year-old, who was married to Sir Richard Branson, died on 24 November last year after suffering a cardiac arrest at the private Lister Hospital in Chelsea, west London.

Senior coroner Professor Fiona Wilcox told Westminster Coroner's Court on Wednesday that Lady Joan did not receive prophylactic anticoagulants at the hospital despite a "very high risk of developing deep vein thrombosis".

"I do find her death would have likely been prevented and the lack of anticoagulation did cause or contribute to her death probably," she said.

The coroner's court heard that Lady Joan was admitted to the hospital on 17 November after a fall weeks earlier on Necker Island, a British Virgin Island owned by her billionaire husband.

She died after suffering a pulmonary embolism, a sudden, dangerous blockage in a lung artery, resulting from deep vein thrombosis.

Haematologist Dr George Adams told the inquest that Lady Joan was "extremely high risk" for blood clots and the "biggest risk factor by far was her immobility and her fracture".

From her hospital admission to her death, Glasgow-born Lady Joan did not receive any prophylactic anticoagulation, which is used to stop blood clots from forming.

The hospital's admitting doctor, Dr Basir Kunduzi, did not complete a bleeding risk assessment on the day of her admission, the inquest heard.

Dr Kunduzi said Lady Joan's death led him to "reflect on my role as a doctor" and the importance of "good communication between team members".

Giving her conclusion, Professor Wilcox said it was "not a case of neglect" and there "wasn't an absence of treatment".

After her death, Sir Richard described his wife as the "shining star around which our family's universe has always orbited".

title: Cancer treatment review finds 'betrayal of trust'
description: Brain cancer patients were prescribed treatment with 'no evidence of benefit' a report has concluded.
fullText:
Brain cancer patients were routinely given extended, non‑standard courses of chemotherapy, with some being misdiagnosed and exposed to serious risks and harm, a review has found.

The Royal College of Physicians (RCP) is investigating 20 cases in which patients in Coventry were prescribed the drug temozolomide (TMZ) for long periods with "little or no evidence of benefit," it said.

Preliminary findings of the review, leaked to the BBC, said staff failings amounted to a "betrayal of patient trust".

University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust said measures had been put in place "to ensure more robust oversight of the prescription and use of TMZ and ensure patient safety".

Stephen Bown from Atherstone, whose son David was prescribed the treatment for eight years, described the review's findings as "incredibly disturbing".

He said his son's health was quickly deteriorating, and believes the treatment he received following a brain tumour operation at the city's University Hospital led to liver problems and muscle pain.

David now lives with his parents and needs round-the-clock care.

"The words they are using are damning of the whole system at Coventry," his father said.

"People knew that what was going on was wrong," he added.

David is one of more than 40 patients represented by lawyers who say they received TMZ for far longer then recommended.

Of the 20 cases reviewed by the RCP, 15 were judged "unsatisfactory overall", meaning care was found to be well below expected standards.

Four were rated as requiring improvements in both clinical and organisational care, while one needed improvement in clinical care alone.

No cases were judged to represent good practice.

There was "scant evidence" of the understanding and documentation of the risks of taking the drug, the review team found.

Guidelines say TMZ should usually be taken post radiotherapy for six cycles, usually over six months.

But many patients have told the BBC they received it for many years – in one case 16 – and believe they suffered physical and emotional harm as a result.

There are a wide range of side effects associated with the drug, including muscle weakness, memory issues and, in rare cases, secondary cancers and liver damage.

According to the letter seen by the BBC, in one case, a patient received more than 100 cycles of TMZ before doctors identified that they had a different, less aggressive type of tumour than originally believed.

The patient later developed acute myeloid leukaemia, a serious blood cancer, after showing signs of bone marrow suppression.

The preliminary findings said there was "insufficient clinical curiosity" in some cases and a lack of collaboration with multidisciplinary team colleagues, allowing potential diagnostic errors to persist.

The letter was "damning" and showed "all levels of oversight failing" at the trust, said Becky Addison of law firm Brabners.

The interim report was sent to the chief medical officer of the NHS trust in April, and has only now been seen by patients, their legal representatives and the BBC.

It was "extremely disappointing" added solicitor apprentice Addison.

"Patients have had so much of their lives taken away from and they deserve answers, and there's still so many more answers that they are yet to be given," she added.

"Personally, I would like the two people at the centre of this report criminally prosecuted," added Bown.

The consultant at the centre of the investigation, referred to as Dr Y but who the BBC understands to be retired consultant Prof Ian Brown, did not participate in the review and failed to attend an interview with investigators.

The review team said it received little information about his clinical outcomes or workload and was unable to explore concerns directly with him.

Former colleagues described Dr Y as difficult to contact and resistant to challenge," the review states.

Investigators heard emails often went unanswered and colleagues frequently struggled to obtain responses about patient care.

Man 'told 13 years of chemotherapy unnecessary'

Doctor accused of over-prescribing chemotherapy drug 'went unchallenged'

'Years of unnecessary chemotherapy stole my youth'

The review team also said he avoided many of the professional and managerial demands expected of him.

It said he did not attend departmental meetings and developed a backlog of patient mortality reviews.

The interim findings also criticise a former clinical nurse specialist - Mr N - describing his working relationship with Dr Y as "very unusual".

Care for the patients was primarily managed and delivered by Mr N, with Dr Y having very limited direct involvement, it was found.

The review team considered that Mr N practised outside of recognised standards, specifically in relation to his:

Failure to ensure that information and advice given to patients was accurate and evidence-based

Failure to ensure properly informed consent and to document it

Delivery of individualised, patient-centred care, including respecting and supporting patients' right to accept or refuse care and treatment

Standard of clinical record keeping

Level of accountability for his actions and in particular his practice as a non-medical prescriber

The findings also questioned why oncology pharmacy teams did not challenge patients receiving oral chemotherapy continuously for 10 to 15 years.

"There were multiple opportunities for scrutiny and challenge," the review found.

"Dr Y appears to have been a difficult individual to engage with, but multiple opportunities for scrutiny and challenge were missed," it added.

The BBC has attempted to contact the two clinicians but has not heard back from them.

Criticising the pharmacy team for failing to raise concerns it said: "Senior pharmacists should have recognised the use of an oral cytotoxic drug for 10-15 years was very unusual… no consideration was given by the pharmacy team to the evidence behind the need for this prolonged temozolomide treatment."

It said: "A lack of awareness of this non-standard prescribing as a defence for inaction was hardly credible."

"I think the most shocking part is everyone knew," added Addison.

"Everyone knew and they didn't speak out.

"They didn't protect patients' interest and they allowed this to happen," she added.

The letter said while progress had been made in the oncology department and pharmacy service, "there was still much work to do to ensure appropriate oversight and to prevent a repetition of the concerns identified."

It said the arrangements remained too reliant on staff self-reporting issues, and the governance of non-medical prescribing was a particular area of weakness requiring "significant improvement."

It made recommendations including independent reviews of all living patients' cases and for the trust to consider whether Mr N should be referred again to the Nursing and Midwifery Council. A previous referral concluded there was no case to answer.

A UHCW spokesperson said all patients receiving TMZ at the time of Dr Y's retirement in 2025 had been reviewed by senior clinicians, "with appropriate care plans put in place".

"We are also undertaking an independent review of our speak up processes, led by an independent party, to ensure staff feel fully supported and confident in raising any concerns.

"The trust will assess the full RCP review when it is published and will take further appropriate action based on its findings.

"We want to reassure our community that patient safety, experience and wellbeing remain our top priorities," the trust added.

title: How to Preorder the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo
description: They will come with Siri AI and a much more powerful battery with up to 45 hours of playback.
fullText:
The latest Apple Event this week revealed two new phones, the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. Pre-orders for the iPhone 18 Pro start on Sep. 12, and for the iPhone Duo, pre-orders start on Oct. 16. There are some nice improvements to the phones, especially the iPhone Duo, which is a long-anticipated foldable model. The iPhones will come with iOS 27, which will bring Siri AI on Monday, Sept. 14.

The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299. The iPhone 18 Pro Max offers the same hardware and features as the 18 Pro on a bigger 6.9-inch display. Check back in on Sept. 12 to pre-order the phones. Apple will start shipping them out on Sept.18.

One of the biggest upgrades you'll notice is the battery. The iPhone 17 had up to 30 hours of playback, and the new 18 Pro comes with up to 45 hours of juice. The new A20 Pro chip has two extra GPU cores, bringing it up to seven cores. The other noticeable difference is in the camera with "Pro controls." There is a new aperture control from a new 48MP "Fusion Telephoto" lens that automatically changes the aperture of the camera to best fit the environment (you can also change it manually). This new lens also improves video with smart focus-tracking (it locks onto a subject in a video); a "Cinematic mode" effect that lets you change the video after shooting to 60 fps for a half-speed video effect; 4K resolution on time-lapse; improved low-light video; and more.

Perhaps the most-anticipated moment of the event was the introduction of the new iPhone Duo. It's a completely new iPhone series and is Apple's first attempt at making a foldable phone. The Duo will be available for pre-order on Sept. 12 and start shipping out on Sept. 18. It starts at a whopping $1,999 with the 256GB version.

The display is 7.6 inches when open and has a 5.4-inch when it's closed. Apple changed the user experience on the Duo, which makes sense since it's the first iPhone with an expandable screen. It seems to be great for multitasking since you can control two apps at once—one on each side of the screen—and you can change it from landscape to portrait mode. It comes with four cameras (two rear, two selfie), Touch ID, and the A20 Pro chip, but it's missing the action button, Pro controls for the camera, and the new Apple Reference Image feature from the iPhone 18 Pro.

title: All the Differences Between the AirPods 5, AirPods 4, and AirPods Pro 3
description: Are the cheaper AirPods 5 a better deal than AirPods Pro 3?
fullText:
I've been rocking the first-gen AirPods Pro since 2021, so you can safely say that I take my time with gadget upgrades. But I was so shocked to see Apple's new AirPods 5 are cheaper and better than the AirPods 4 that I initially thought I might've just found the easier upgrade decision of all time. But then, my sense of propriety kicked in: Experience has taught me to weigh my options carefully before buying anything, so I decided to compare (on paper, at least) the AirPods 5 with their counterparts from Apple: the AirPods 4 with active noise cancellation (ANC) and the AirPods Pro 3. Here's what I found.

As much as I want to love the AirPods 5, and as much as I appreciate the fact that ANC is now standard on all Apple earbuds, the new model's noise cancellation feature is significantly weaker than that on the AirPods Pro 3. According to the specs comparison on Apple's website, the AirPods Pro 3 has "3x more Active Noise Cancellation (ANC) than AirPods 5." This is the most important AirPods feature for me, and I'm seriously considering paying that $120 premium (at retail) for better ANC. Having said that, the AirPods 5 do get "1.5x more ANC than AirPods 4 (with ANC)," so it could be a good upgrade for many people.

According to Apple, the AirPods 5 offer up to five hours of battery on a single charge (with ANC on), and 22 hours of battery life if you include the power from the charging case. If you get the cheapest variant of the AirPods 5 (without wireless charging), these numbers drop to four hours on one charge, and 20 hours from the charging case. This is lower than the AirPods 4 (with ANC), which offer 5 hours of battery life and 30 hours including the charging case. The AirPods Pro 3 have the best battery life, with 8 hours of playback time on a single charge and 24 hours with the charging case.

If you opt for the $149 variant of the AirPods 5, you're getting improved battery life, on-stem volume controls, a wireless charging case, and a speaker for Find My. I think those features are easily worth the extra $20 over the base variant of the AirPods 5. I think the extra hour of battery life is an essential feature, and all the others are great quality-of-life additions. It's nice to control volume by swiping the stem of the AirPods, and after switching to wireless charging last year, I can't see myself going back. The case's speaker, which plays a sound and allows you to locate it when it disappears into your couch, might be worth the cost all on its own.

The AirPods Pro 3's ear tips rest in your ear canal. This is optimal for ensuring the best noise cancellation and a secure fit, but it doesn't work for everyone. I know quite a few people who prefer the AirPods 4's design, where the earbuds rest outside the ear canal. The AirPods 5 follow the same design language and may be the better choice for some people.

You can use your AirPods Pro 3 as a temporary hearing aid, but that doesn't extend to the AirPods 5 or the AirPods 4. If you need Apple's hearing health features, you should choose the AirPods Pro 3, which have been cleared by the FDA for use as a hearing-aid.

title: Harfield's 'surreal' return after 717-day injury lay-off
description: Aldershot Town defender Ollie Harfield talks about his return to action after a serious knee injury.
fullText:
Aldershot Town defender Ollie Harfield says that his return to action after a serious knee injury that saw him miss 717 days was a "surreal experience".

The 28-year-old tore ligaments and dislocated his knee during a National League match in September 2024 where there was a fear he could lose his leg.

Harfield was told by nine people that his footballing career was over, but defied those odds as he made his return to the pitch on Tuesday night.

The full-back started for the Shots against West Ham U21s in the National League Cup, playing just over 30 minutes before leaving the pitch to a standing ovation.

"It was unbelievable to be honest and a surreal experience for me," Harfield told BBC Radio Surrey.

"It's something that I've been thinking about for nearly two years now to do it last night was unbelievable.

"I got an amazing ovation when I came out and then obviously when I came off in the 34th minute it was just everything that I've dreamed of over the last two years and I just can't wait to do it in a proper National League game with a full stadium."

Harfield has documented his recovery from the serious knee injury on his TikTok account, with the initial video of his injury gaining more than 13 million views.

The top comment on that video is from Tottenham midfielder James Maddison who was wishing him luck in his recovery.

Harfield joined Aldershot in 2022 from Weymouth and has made 96 appearances, registering 10 assists.

In the video where he sustained his injury he is seen challenging for a ball with a York City player before falling to the floor and immediately calling for help.

The oposition player comes to Harfield's aid before clutching his head in disbelief having caught sight of his disfigured knee.

"My leg just got caught in the ground in a 50-50 and I went down and I saw my leg was facing the wrong way," Harfield added.

"I was obviously rushed straight to hospital and realised that I'd ruptured everything possible, broken multiple bones and found out I could have lost my leg in the injury.

"It was a really bad injury, but it's just amazing to be here now and over the other side of it, to be honest."

title: Hewett and Reid into last eight of US Open singles
description: British duo Alfie Hewett and Gordon Reid win their respective first-round matches in the men's wheelchair singles at the US Open.
fullText:
British duo Alfie Hewett and Gordon Reid both reached the men's wheelchair singles quarter-finals at the US Open on Wednesday.

Hewett, the number two seed and a four-time winner in New York, dropped only two games in a 6-0 6-2 victory against Spain's Daniel Caverzaschi and will face American Casey Ratzlaff for a place in the semi-finals.

Reid's match against Frenchman Stephane Houdet was a much closer contest, with the Scot eventually winning 6-3 5-7 6-2 in two hours and 13 minutes.

Up next for Reid is the defending champion and top seed Tokito Oda of Japan, who has won the past six Grand Slam singles titles.

Hewett and Reid are also attempting to win a sixth US Open wheelchair doubles title together as a pairing and won their opening round on Tuesday, with a semi-final against Oda and Argentina's Gustavo Fernandez to come.

Meanwhile, Andy Lapthorne and Greg Slade were beaten in the first round of the quad singles on Wednesday.

Lapthorne lost 6-2 6-1 to top seed Niels Vink of the Netherlands, while Slade was defeated 6-4 6-2 by Gonzalo Lazarte of Argentina.

Lapthorne is still involved in the quad doubles competition and is into the semi-finals alongside South African partner Leon Els.

title: Prince William launches sport mental health toolkit
description: Prince William urges sport at every level to make suicide prevention part of its culture through a new nationwide toolkit called On Your Side.
fullText:
Prince William has urged sport at every level to make suicide prevention part of its culture through a new nationwide toolkit.

Launched by the Prince of Wales and the Royal Foundation, On Your Side, external is a set of resources available online that aims "to make suicide prevention as much a part of sport as warm-up, training and performance".

The project is backed by more than 70 organisations including the Football Association, Premier League, Team GB, British Cycling and a host of leading mental health charities.

"Through my work on mental health, I have met people whose lives have been changed forever by suicide," said Prince William. "But I have also met people whose lives have been saved because someone stepped in to help."

The 44-year-old Royal, who has previously spoken about his own struggles with mental health issues, said that while he acknowledges the good work being done by current services, too often "initiatives are fragmented" and "support is inconsistent, particularly at a grassroots level".

William added that he hopes On Your Side provides everyone involved in sport who notices someone is struggling the "clear, practical guidance" to help that person find the support they need.

On Your Side is being launched to coincide with World Suicide Prevention Day on 10 September.

William says it has taken 'long time to understand my emotions'

According to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), there were 6,190 suicides registered in England and Wales in 2024.

It remains the biggest cause of death for men under the age of 50 and the rate remains notably higher among males (17.6 per 100,000 people) than females (5.7 per 100,000).

A promotional video for On Your Side features England men's football captain Harry Kane, F1 driver George Russell and Women's Rugby World Cup winner Rochelle 'Rocky' Clark.

The toolkit will officially be launched at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium, a venue chosen because its construction included a 'talking bench' in memory of former player Gary Speed.

Ex-Wales captain and manager Speed, who also played for Leeds, Bolton, Newcastle and Sheffield United, took his own life in November 2011.

Premier League record goalscorer and Match of the Day pundit Alan Shearer, who was a close friend of Speed, is among the athletes to have given their backing to the initiative.

"For me, this is obviously very personal," said Shearer.

"We can't always know when somebody is struggling, but we can all be better at asking, listening, and helping someone find the right support.

"You don't have to be an expert. You don't have to have all the answers, but I hope that everyone in sport will use the toolkit."

Prince William said he wants On Your Side to take advantage of sport's "remarkable ability to bring people together".

He added: "In moments of need, the right support can make all the difference. We all have the power to help, and that's why suicide prevention must be an important part of everyday sporting life."

The National Health Service, the Samaritans and mental health charity Mind were all consulted during the creation of On Your Side.

The Royal Foundation said the project had taken two years to complete and added that, although it was being launched to coincide with World Suicide Prevention Day, the initiative is "not a one-day campaign" and hopes it will have a long-lasting legacy.

If you, or someone you know, has been affected by any of the issues in this article, then support and information is available at BBC Action Line.

title: Benn 'dragged down to pits of hell' by weight cut
description: Conor Benn says making the welterweight limit for his world-title challenge against Ryan Garcia has felt like being "dragged down to the pits of hell" but insists he is healthy and will make weight.
fullText:
Conor Benn says making the welterweight limit for his world title challenge against Ryan Garcia has felt like being "dragged down to the pits of hell" but insists he is healthy and will make weight.

Benn, 29, faces WBC champion Garcia at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas on Saturday in the first world title fight of his 10-year professional career.

The Briton must weigh no more than 10st 7lb (67kg) when he steps on the scales in on Friday, having not made the welterweight limit for more than four years.

"It's been extremely difficult," Benn told BBC Sport.

"It feels like I've been dragged down to the pits of hell, had a fight with Satan and God brought me back to life.

"Making weight has been the hardest thing I've done. I haven't made weight for four and a half years so it's going to be hard.

"But I won't moan when I'm getting paid a fortune to headline in Vegas for a world title. I know what I signed up for."

Benn last made the welterweight limit when stopping Chris van Heerden in two rounds in April 2022.

He stepped up to 11st 6lb (73kg) for two lucrative contests with Chris Eubank Jr last year, suffering the first defeat of his professional career in April 2025 before avenging the loss on points seven months later.

Benn's appearance in pictures and videos posted on social media during fight week has prompted concern among some observers over the effects of dropping back to welterweight.

Former world champion Carl Froch and Benn's former opponent Chris Algieri are among those to have questioned whether the weight cut could leave him depleted.

It is particularly pertinent given the contrasting styles on Saturday. Benn is an aggressive, front-foot fighter who likes to apply pressure, while American Garcia, 28, possesses fast hands and is renowned for a dangerous counter left hook.

But Benn dismissed concerns over his condition.

"I'm healthy," he said, adding that he expects to rehydrate significantly and enter the ring at around 12st 7lb (80kg) - two stones heavier than the welterweight limit.

Even if he fulfils a lifelong ambition by winning a maiden world title and following in his father Nigel's footsteps, Benn intends to vacate the belt "straight away" and move back up to middleweight or potentially as high as super-middleweight.

"I love challenges and that's what life is about, otherwise it's boring," he added.

For all the difficulty presented by the weight cut, there was little outward sign of Benn being weighed down by the occasion.

He was relaxed and in good spirits as he made time for the travelling British media at the UFC's Meta Apex, with father and British boxing great Nigel Benn by his side.

The former two-weight world champion has been a prominent presence throughout fight week, despite previously suggesting he would take a step back from his son's career.

One man Conor Benn is yet to see, however, is his opponent.

Garcia did not appear for a scheduled face-off at Mandalay Bay on Tuesday, with Benn told beforehand that the champion would not be attending.

Benn turned up regardless and jokingly squared up to his 62-year-old father instead.

He described Garcia as a "strange geezer" and said the no-show had done the champion "no favours".

"I'm not bothered, I've dealt with worse," Conor Benn added. "If he turns up or not, it makes no difference to me.

"Irrespective of how hard the weight cut is or anything else, we owe it to the public to give the fans what they want. It's a lack of discipline and professionalism."

title: Selby defeats Zhang to progress at English Open
description: World number two Mark Selby progresses to the third round of the English Open by winning a deciding frame against China's Zhang Anda.
fullText:
World number two Mark Selby progressed to the third round of the English Open by winning a deciding frame against China's Zhang Anda.

Selby completed a final clearance of 39 to win the final frame 59-49, taking victory on the black.

Zhang had levelled the tie at 3-3 with a century break, after Selby has turned round a 2-1 deficit to lead 3-2.

The 43-year-old will now meet Kyren Wilson, who won 4-3 against Wuhan Open champion Chang Bingyu, in the last 16 in Brentwood.

Oliver Lines, who defeated world number one Zhao Xintong in the first round, exited the competition with a 4-3 defeat to Yuan Sijun, losing the last two frames having pulled back from 2-0 down to lead 3-2.

World number three Judd Trump moved into the third round with a 4-1 win over Ashley Carty and will play Anthony McGill, who defeated Fan Zhengyi 4-1.

Barry Hawkins beat Daniel Wells 4-1 to set-up a tie with Mark Williams, who triumphed 4-3 over Matthew Selt, while Wu Yize sealed a 4-2 victory over compatriot Xu Si and will now face Liam Davies, who took a 4-1 win against Xinbo Wang.

Shaun Murphy and Ali Carter were the only 4-0 victors in the round, beating Jamie Clarke and Robbie Williams respectively.

title: Arsenal are passing every test - and Odegaard is in form of his life
description: Another Arsenal win, another Martin Odegaard goal - the Gunners captain looks back to his best, writes Phil McNulty.
fullText:
Arsenal were one game away from the dream double of Premier League and Champions League last season, even with the brilliance of Martin Odegaard diminished by injuries and indifferent form.

As they look to go one better than that fully merited first Premier League title in 24 years, Arsenal and manager Mikel Arteta will be thrilled to see the 27-year-old Norwegian starting the new campaign in the form of his life.

If they could win the title and only lose to Paris St-Germain on penalties in the Champions League final with Odegaard in those reduced circumstances, what can Arsenal achieve with their captain already stamping his authority so significantly domestically and in Europe?

Arsenal dominated Napoli in the opening game of their Champions League campaign, but it still took Odegaard to make the decisive contribution with a stunning left-foot strike 15 minutes from time to secure a 1-0 win.

It seems, with Odegaard in this form, Arsenal can overcome every test to make anything possible for Arteta's team.

Odegaard was troubled by knee and shoulder injuries last season, restricting him to only 36 games in all competitions, scoring just one goal with seven assists. He only played in 24 Premier League matches as Arsenal finally lifted the crown.

He showed signs of a revival as Norway reached the World Cup quarter-final, losing to England, but has moved on to a different level in the opening phase of this season.

Odegaard hits Arsenal winner to sink Napoli - report & ratings

Odegaard gave a flavour of what was to come in the Community Shield win against Manchester City in Cardiff with an audacious final goal in Arsenal's 3-0 win, sitting down keeper Gianluigi Donnarumma before passing the ball into an empty net.

He scored in the 3-0 victory against Coventry City, also scoring the winner as Arsenal came from behind to beat Chelsea 2-1 at Emirates Stadium to maintain their 100% start.

Odegaard scored after a perfectly timed, intelligent run into the box that allowed him to step on to Kai Havertz's clever dummy before sending an emphatic finish past Chelsea keeper Emiliano Martinez.

This, and his winner in Naples, was the work of a lavishly gifted player finally operating at the peak of his powers once more, fully fit and playing in a team overflowing with the confidence and self-belief long-awaited success has given them.

It was a win Arsenal needed, because they face some tough Champions League assignments on the road ahead, such as a home game with Real Madrid and a visit to Bayern Munich.

The manner in which they patiently broke down Napoli's resistance, with the Serie A side utilising a defensive shield straight from veteran coach Max Allegri's well-thumbed playbook, showed calmness and maturity.

In every act this season, Arsenal already look like a side ready to build on their achievements of last term.

Odegaard, as manager Arteta hinted, is almost playing like someone with something to prove, knowing himself that while Arsenal had a season of glory last time out, his personal contribution was not what he expected from himself.

Former Premier League defender Nedum Onuoha, a pundit on Wednesday's Match of the Day, said Odegaard "will want to have a bigger impact on the team this season".

"They have got unfinished business in the Champions League," said Onuoha. "He wants to be the first captain of Arsenal to lift that trophy.

"You would not back against them winning it based on what we've seen them do in this competition in the past two seasons, but he 100% takes Arsenal to a different level when he is on form and playing like this.

"That's the way it should be as well. I think when he is at his best, Arsenal are at their best.

"I think there have been times when he's not been at his best and as a team they can still look good and win games, but the best version of Arsenal in my opinion comes when Odegaard is pulling the strings, because so many other players will be involved in the way they attack, and the way they attack will look different at certain points."

This time around, Odegaard looks smooth as silk – and it is no coincidence Arsenal look exactly the same.

"This is what we need: players with that mindset to decide the game, to play with that personality and keep taking risks," said Arteta. "He is getting into those positions much 

In Naples, Odegaard not only settled the game but set the tone, working tirelessly as the perfect of example of leadership as well as being the match winner.

"Arsenal have obviously looked good at the start of the season and he has been a big reason for that," added Onuoha. "Some of his creativity, especially on the right-hand side, has been excellent.

"He looks after the ball so well. He is always looking for that pass to be able to create opportunities and he even does the defensive work as well."

Odegaard succeeded where other team-mates failed, Arsenal missing several clear-cut opportunities before he struck.

Arsenal's superiority was illustrated by having 26 shots, their most in a single Champions League match since records started being kept in 2003-04. It was also the most Napoli have faced in that time.

"Martin is contributing with goals that are impacting results which is what we want from our attacking players, being decisive," said Arteta. "We should have done it in a different way because of the amount of chances we created."

The Champions League has proved elusive for Arsenal, with finals lost to Barcelona in 2006 and to PSG last season.

It remains their Holy Grail – but if Odegaard maintains his brilliant form then their chances of crossing a so far insurmountable barrier will increase hugely.

title: Star subs rescue Chelsea as Alonso 'takes blame'
description: Chelsea get the better of Leeds in a cup thriller, but Blues boss Xabi Alonso has food for thought after needing rescue act from his star substitutes.
fullText:
Xabi Alonso watched his Chelsea team hit six goals in the second half against Leeds United but felt the need to "take responsibility" for the shaky start that came before the thrilling flurry.

Amid jubilation that followed the final whistle at Stamford Bridge, where Chelsea recovered from 2-0 down to progress as 6-3 winners in the Carabao Cup, it was easy to forget that Alonso's side were booed off at half-time.

Supporters witnessed arguably the worst first half of Alonso's short tenure to date, with Chelsea fortunate not to be further in arrears after the head coach made nine changes to his line-up.

The team's rhythm was disrupted. Leeds made eight changes themselves, but Daniel Farke's side took control and were threatening to surge into the fourth round.

Defender Tarik Muharemovic opened the scoring before Brenden Aaronson doubled Leeds' lead shortly after the break.

Alonso had responded to Chelsea's out-of-sorts start by making four substitutions at half-time. On came Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers, Pedro Neto and Reece James, and together they changed the game.

The sight of Palmer and Rogers warming up had gladdened the hearts of many, turning jeers to cheers. By the end of the night, Palmer had scored twice, fellow substitute Neto had also found the net, and Rogers left the field after helping to create four goals from open play in Chelsea's remarkable turnaround.

However, speaking after the match, Alonso said he had made it "hard" for his players in the first place.

"I need to take my own blame and my own responsibility on the things that happen," he said. "I need to be able to help them better so they are not responsible, and after you need to react and think what's better for the team."

Alonso said the raft of substitutions he felt compelled to make should be considered "part of the game".

Chelsea come back to thump Leeds 6-3 in EFL Cup third round

For the Premier League's biggest clubs, this competition is usually an opportunity to blood youngsters and give fringe players valuable minutes.

However, only 35-year-old Danny Welbeck, who scored twice, emerged from the starters with a compelling case for more regular involvement.

Even Valentin Barco, despite scoring Chelsea's fifth goal, was partly at fault for Leeds' second and was among several players who repeatedly surrendered possession during a difficult first half.

Young attackers Estevao Willian and Jamie Gittens suffered the disappointment of being substituted at half-time, while £40m signing Geovany Quenda, who joined from Sporting, did not add to his solitary substitute appearance for the club as he watched from the bench.

Midfielder Reggie Watson, making his debut at the age of 16, was also withdrawn at the break after being booked.

Alonso later said he would not take a "cynical" view as some on the outside might about the difference in level between his proven stars and Chelsea's back-up options.

He added: "I know that probably I have to take the right decisions for them to show their best level, so it's something that I will analyse and learn from today."

Nevertheless, reaching the fourth round is important for Chelsea.

It is not only about preserving their hopes of silverware in a season without European football, but Chelsea are also a club that need as many competitive fixtures as possible.

They have a 27-man squad, supported by a strong academy pipeline, and these matches are vital for keeping a large group of players engaged throughout the campaign.

There is an irony, then, that Palmer, Rogers and Chelsea's other established stars may have secured future opportunities for the very fringe players whose performances had put the club's EFL Cup campaign at risk.

title: Liverpool will reward Mac Allister if he lets his football do talking
description: After saying he was "very sad" at the lack of a contract offer from Liverpool, Alexis Mac Allister proved his worth against Atletico Madrid.
fullText:
The sheer ferocity of the strike to beat Jan Oblak was one thing, but the raw emotion shown by Alexis Mac Allister as he grabbed the Liverpool badge on his shirt and celebrated in front of the Kop told you all that you needed to know.

Just a day earlier, Mac Allister had spoken with a different kind of emotion inside the press room at Anfield as he expressed his sadness at Liverpool not offering him a new contract during the summer.

The Argentine, who is currently contracted until 2028, spoke passionately about his love for the club and the city and how he didn't feel like he had anything to prove - but there was an admittance that he needed to show the level he knew he could perform at.

Thankfully for Andoni Iraola and Liverpool, Mac Allister did just that by letting his football do the talking in their 2-1 win over Atletico Madrid.

From the outset against Diego Simeone's side, the midfielder seemed like a man on a mission. He blazed over early on from outside the box then picked up a booking just before the half-hour mark. Seeing Simeone wave an imaginary yellow card when he wanted a second booking for his compatriot just before half-time told a story in itself.

Simeone could only watch on when Mac Allister's left foot connected with the ball from outside the box and leave a diving Oblak with no chance - turning the game on its head after Marcos Llorente's opening goal and Dominik Szoboszlai's equaliser.

It wasn't quite like the strike that produced an actual seismic event - reaching a peak magnitude of 1.74 on the Richter scale - when Mac Allister found the top corner against Tottenham in 2025 on the day Liverpool won the Premier League, but it was more than good enough to beat one of the best goalkeepers in the world.

Mac Allister scores winner as Liverpool beat Atletico Madrid - report and ratings

Mac Allister 'sad' at no Liverpool contract offer

And it was certainly what Iraola and the Anfield hierarchy would have wanted to see after a below-par campaign from Mac Allister last season.

The understanding is that they were of the belief that Mac Allister's performances did not warrant the offer of fresh terms.

But if he can carry on like this, then it will be a question of when rather than if that offer is made for whoever replaces Richard Hughes - even if Mac Allister said he didn't know if his goal would boost his chances of a new contract.

"It was a lovely goal from Alexis and a lovely goal from Dominik Szoboszlai. It is good the midfielders can add goals," said Iraola, who smartly navigated a question about Mac Allister's future.

"We have midfielders that naturally they are going to arrive to the box - it is inside them and it is good we can also benefit offensively."

Former England goalkeeper Paul Robinson said on BBC Radio 5 Live it was "exactly what Mac Allister needed to do".

"If you don't get offered a new contract there's a reason, so what do you do? You go out and earn it," said Robinson.

"You work hard, you play to your level and he did that. He put himself about and popped up with a wonderful strike."

Five of Mac Allister's 20 goals for Liverpool in all competitions have now come from outside the penalty area.

Steven Gerrard knows more than most about playing in midfield and scoring from distance for Liverpool and he described Mac Allister's performance as "outstanding".

"Let your football do the talking," said Gerrard on TNT Sports. "Consistency, top performance, show your experience. Show you're a top international. This club will reward you."

Mac Allister himself said how it was a "positive step" for Liverpool as they won for the first time at Anfield this season on what was Iraola's debut as a manager in the Champions League.

"It was a good comeback," said Mac Allister on TNT Sports. "Overall, it was a good performance. Now we have to think about the next one.

"Before the game we spoke about the beginning of the first half and second half. I liked the mentality.

"I think we showed desire today. We got the fans behind us and that's really important when you play at Anfield. A positive step for us."

Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock said Mac Allister just needed to be put into a system that suits him to get the best out of him.

"I don't think he has to show his importance to Liverpool, I think everyone knows the qualities he has got anyway," said Warnock, who was a pundit on Wednesday's Match of the Day.

"I think there will be a lot of talk about him because of what has gone on in the past few days, but I think Liverpool fans were already asking why hasn't he been offered a new contract when other players have.

"To come out and talk about a contract situation like he did, a couple of days before a game, and to be able to back it up the way he did with a good performance is important - but it is over the course of the season, where his performances are important because if he wants a contract and he thinks he deserves a contract then if his performances are good, he will get one.

"We all know the qualities that he has got - he is a World Cup winner, a Premier League winner, we know that he's a very good player, it is just he has got to be put into the right system to make it work.

"At the moment Liverpool's system is a little bit dysfunctional but it is starting to get better and he will get better because of that."

title: Gauff saves match points to set up Rybakina semi-final
description: Coco Gauff saves two match points to beat Mirra Andreeva and set up a US Open semi-final against incoming world number one Elena Rybakina.
fullText:
Coco Gauff saved two match points as she fought from a set down to beat Mirra Andreeva and set up a US Open semi-final against incoming world number one Elena Rybakina.

Blown away in a 26-minute opening set, fourth seed Gauff was twice pegged back from a break up in a scrappy second set before coming through a 16-point tie-break to force a decider.

Roared on by a partisan crowd, the American's resilience proved the difference in what became a mental battle as she closed out a 2-6 7-6 (9-7) 6-2 win – a performance she said was inspired by compatriot Frances Tiafoe's comeback victory over Alex Michelsen on Tuesday night.

Progression to the last four marks back-to-back Grand Slam semi-finals for the two-time major champion and her first in New York since winning the title in 2023.

It is the first time the top four seeds have reached the semi-finals of the women's singles at a major since Wimbledon in 2009, after top seed Sabalenka and third seed Jessica Pegula progressed on Tuesday.

"At the end of the first set I was thinking about Frances and how he came back yesterday," Gauff said.

"We all want to do well in front of this crowd. Honestly, I was just trying to leave the court with no regrets."

Gauff also drew strength from her home crowd, something she has learned to embrace having struggled with the pressure of "disappointing" them with a "bad match" earlier in her career.

"I don't have that fear of disappointing them. I'm just using them and knowing that when I step on this court, they're still going to have my back," she said.

Earlier, second seed Rybakina recovered from losing a set for the first time this tournament - and going break-point down in the decider - to beat Zheng Qinwen 3-6 6-1 6-4.

The 27-year arrived at the US Open trailing Aryna Sabalenka by just 434 points and was guaranteed to secure the number one ranking for the first time in her career by reaching the semi-finals.

'Just a number' - Rybakina's rise to world number one

Rybakina reaches #1 as Gauff completes epic semis line-up

This was an uncharacteristic performance from Gauff, whose 22 winners were vastly outnumbered by 42 unforced errors, including 12 double faults.

She won just five of the opening 21 points as Andreeva breezed into a one-set lead and later failed to consolidate breaks at 4-2 and 5-3 in the second set.

A double fault at the beginning of the tie-break felt ominous, but the 22-year-old maintained her composure to save two match points - something which proved a turning point as she dominated the clutch moments in the decider.

Her response was in stark contrast to Andreeva, who struck 14 unforced errors to Gauff's two in the final set and flung a racquet in frustration following the first break of serve.

"You have to admire how Coco does this. She's done it so many times in her career," former British number one Annabel Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"She's unrecognisable from the player at the start of this match. She was subdued and playing defensive tennis. By the end, she was completely controlling the match.

"We've been blessed with the amount of intriguing matches we've had. You're seeing these warriors out on court.

"It's the ability of one of the gladiators to get themselves back in it."

Addressing her outburst, Andreeva said: "I felt like I was holding my emotions for too long, not reacting on a lot of points. At one point I felt like needed to let it out."

Rybakina's ascension to the top of the rankings – the first Kazakhstani man or woman to do so – will rightly dominate the headlines.

She has achieved one of her two goals for the tournament and is now just two wins away from a second major title of the season, having won the Australian Open in January.

However, beaten opponent Zheng's achievements should not go unnoticed, offering a welcome reminder of her talent with an entertaining run to the last eight.

Having dropped out of the top 100 following elbow surgery in July 2025, the reigning Olympic champion navigated three qualifying rounds before registering her first Grand Slam main-draw win since last year's French Open.

She later stunned 22nd seed Madison Keys, who she trailed 5-0 in the third set and saved match point, and eighth seed Iga Swiatek to reach her third quarter-final in New York.

Ranked 121st heading into the tournament, she is now up to 52nd in the live rankings and has just 65 points to defend for the remainder of the season.

But for all the positives, there is an unshakable sense of what might have been against Rybakina.

Momentum was with the 23-year-old after she broke late in the first set before staving off five break points to take a 1-0 lead. However, she was completely blown away in the second set, with her second serve coming under considerable pressure.

She earned a break point in the eighth game of the decider but missed a routine backhand pass. In the next game, she brilliantly fought back from 0-40 to deuce but then followed a loose backhand with a double fault as her hopes of a maiden US Open semi-final slipped away.

title: Nicolas Cage's driveway collapses as sinkhole opens up at his Malibu home
description: A 30ft crater opened up outside the actor's home in Malibu after heavy rain in Southern California.
fullText:
A large sinkhole has opened up up outside a house in Malibu reportedly belonging to Hollywood actor Nicolas Cage.

The sinkhole, estimated to be 30ft (9.1m) by 30ft, appeared after the driveway collapsed and follows heavy rain in southern California over recent days.

Local media said that no injuries had been reported. BBC News has asked representatives for Cage for comment.

The actor bought the home in 2024, according to a report in the New York Times shortly after the sale.

Cage won an Oscar for Leaving Las Vegas and is also known for films such as Gone in 60 Seconds, Face/Off and Con Air, as well as Pig, Moonstruck and The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent.

Nearby residents said they were informed that an 8ft sinkhole had begun forming on Monday.

"At that point, the homeowners were not overly concerned," one resident told Los Angeles magazine.

"We thought it could be fixed pretty quickly." But then, he continued, "all hell broke loose".

Further ground gave way in the early hours of Tuesday morning, leaving a 30ft crater.

The collapse was said to swallow up much of the home's driveway, and left broken asphalt, concrete and construction debris inside the hole.

Emergency services responded in the early hours of Tuesday morning when the structural failure caused a gas leak. SoCalGas later confirmed the leak had been secured.

Traffic cones have been placed around the crater, and AFP reported that waves pounding the sea front can be seen "lapping in the hole and rushing out again under the stanchions that support the home".

The damage occurred after a Los Angeles coastal flooding warning was issued linked to Tropical Storm Marie, which was previously a hurricane.

While the hurricane had remained offshore, it was said to have brought rain and high waves to Southern California.

Malibu City officials have declared at least five homes on the street unsafe for entry and warned residents that emergency access is "severely constrained", and that the area "may be impassable due to the large portion of the road that has collapsed".

title: As midterms approach, new poll finds that few Americans trust campaigns or Trump
description: Americans are more skeptical of government information than they were a few years ago, with majorities now saying they have little or no trust in federal government information about elections and pol...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Americans are more skeptical of government information than they were a few years ago, with majorities now saying they have little or no trust in federal government information about elections and politics, foreign affairs or the environment, a new poll finds.

The survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and USAFacts shows that while mistrust of government information has grown since 2024, it's also higher than it was at the end of President Donald Trump's first term, underscoring how his recent attempts to dismantle parts of the federal bureaucracy may have affected public confidence in the executive branch, particularly among Democrats.

Those suspicions extend to the results of the coming midterm elections. Only 34% of U.S. adults trust government certifications of election results "a great deal" or "quite a bit," which is down slightly from 40% in 2024. Certification is a typically routine process in which local and state officials confirm the vote count, but it's become politicized since Trump lost the 2020 presidential election.

Trust in government information has also become more partisan since Trump's first term, the survey found.

"It's pretty hard to trust anything that's being communicated," said Shannon Ingram, 46, a Democrat who lives in Maryland, pointing to shifting health recommendations as an example of "questionable" government information she's seen since Trump regained office. "There is a significant amount of bias, and it comes from the people who are authoring the content."

About 6 in 10 U.S. adults have low trust in information from the federal government about the environment, foreign affairs, elections and politics, abortion or immigration — saying they trust it "only a little" or "not at all."

Mistrust in what the federal government says has risen at least slightly on nearly every topic that was asked about in an AP-NORC/ USAFacts survey from 2019. That includes education — which has risen from 37% in 2019 to 53% now — with a 9-percentage point spike in the last year.

The findings come after a year and a half of upheaval in the executive branch. Trump began to dismantle key parts of the federal bureaucracy soon after entering the White House for the second time, moving to end longstanding programs and shutter entire agencies.

Since then, thousands of federal employees have been fired or left their jobs, substantially reducing the ranks of the government statisticians and leading experts to warn about risks to data quality.

Shifting regulations and recommendations have also led to dramatic changes in government policy. Recent changes to longstanding health advice have put doctors and medical organizations at odds with the Trump administration on vaccination recommendations. Earlier this year, the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded a scientific finding that has underpinned government action to fight climate change for more than a decade.

Jeremy Cove, a 44-year-old Republican from Missouri, trusts the Trump administration's guidance on matters like vaccines, but he disagrees with their assertion that climate change is not happening, or that humans are not contributing to it.

"I love Trump; I voted for Trump, but some of the things he's doing just makes me distrust more," Cove said. "Stuff like renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America, it just makes you think about what their priorities are. Then you realize it's not what it should be, which in turn, makes you distrust even more."

The gap between Republicans' and Democrats' trust in government information is much wider than it was during Trump's first term, a shift that first began to appear under former President Joe Biden.

Democrats were generally less likely to trust government information in Trump's first term, but not dramatically more than Republicans. That shifted when control of the White House changed hands. Republicans' mistrust in government information rose while Biden was president and fell after Trump took office. Meanwhile, Democrats' doubts declined under Biden and spiked when Trump regained power.

For example, 61% of Democrats now have low trust in information about the federal budget, compared with 42% of Republicans, while 60% of Democrats have low trust in information about crime, compared with only 32% of Republicans.

Larry Haith, a 76-year-old Republican from Idaho, says he tends to trust the federal government — though, he acknowledges that it can vary based on the current administration.

"Generally speaking, I've got more confidence in the federal government today than I've had in years," he said.

Independents, meanwhile, became more mistrustful of government information under Biden and haven't shifted under Trump.

The only issue without a substantial partisan divide in the new survey is vaccination recommendations and safety: about 6 in 10 Democrats, Republicans and independents trust the federal government on vaccination recommendations and safety "only a little" or "not at all."

As the 2026 midterms approach, public concern about the accuracy of the election results is widespread. Just under half of U.S. adults are "extremely" or "very" concerned the federal government will publicly discredit or question election results, tamper with election results, or pressure state election officials to change how they certify or report results.

Over the past few months, Trump has repeated long-debunked allegations of mass voter fraud in the 2020 election, attempted to place new restrictions on mail voting in time for the midterms and pushed Congress to enact a proof-of-citizenship requirement to register and vote. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has also warned state officials that they could lose funding or face investigations if they fail to go along with Trump's election security demands.

At the same time, few Americans trust the information they get from political campaigns. Only about 1 in 10 U.S. adults say the Democratic Party or Republican Party campaign messages are "always" or "often" based in factual information.

In a sign of how deep the mistrust runs, only about one-quarter of Democrats trust their party's campaign messages to be factual at least "often," while a similar share of Republicans say this about their party.

Less than half of Democrats, 44%, trust government certifications of election results "a great deal" or "quite a bit," a substantial decline from 65% in 2024.

Even with Trump back in the White House, though, Republicans haven't seen a similar increase in confidence. Only 29% of Republicans have high trust in government certifications of election results, up just slightly from 2024.

Trust in other sources of information about election outcomes — such as national news outlets or cable news networks — is also low overall.

Kim Murza, a Democrat from Colorado, has faith in the country's ability to run fair elections but blames the Trump administration for eroding Americans' trust in the process.

"My concern is more about what the current administration is doing," said 45-year-old Murza. "I think they are doing whatever they can to try to put that distrust in people's minds."

The AP-NORC/ USAFacts poll of 1,036 adults was conducted July 29 to Aug. 10 using a sample drawn from NORC's probability-based AmeriSpeak Panel, which is designed to be representative of the U.S. population. The margin of sampling error for adults overall is plus or minus 4.1 percentage points. The margin of sampling error is plus or minus 6.4 for Republicans overall and plus or minus 6.0 for Democrats overall.

title: Kelsey Grammer says Trump may go down as one of the best presidents
description: While Trump’s approval ratings remain underwater, 'Frasier' star Kelsey Grammer offered a more favorable assessment in a recent interview.
fullText:
As President Donald Trump's unpopularity with the American public continues to be reflected in approval polls, Kelsey Grammer has a much rosier outlook, saying in a recent interview that the president will be remembered as one of the best in U.S. history.

In a recent interview with the British talk radio station LBC, the Republican "Frasier" star said Trump loved America and predicted the president will "probably" be remembered as one of the best leaders in the country's history.

"Because nobody really stood up for America in quite some time in the presidency," Grammer said.

Grammer, 71, also praised how he perceives Trump responds to critics.

"He says if somebody comes at him, if they come at him with hate, which they really have done, he just sends it right back at them," he said. "And I think that throws them off."

Grammer's comments also follow an interview in Us Weekly, published June 24, in which he admitted that he has "wrestled" with the idea of running for political office.

"I would consider it. It would possibly tick that box for me, in terms of the service I feel I should have given to my fellow man – to my fellow countrymen – that I missed in the military," Grammer said. "Maybe (running for office) would be the way to do it."

The "Cheers" actor previously claimed that being a registered Republican is the "worst thing you can be" in the entertainment industry, saying during a February appearance on the Megyn Kelly Show that "I've lost some friends through the last few years, but I've gained others." He added he believes it's "not popular" for people with different political values to find middle ground.

Despite Grammer's prediction of Trump's legacy, recent national polls offer a less-than-stellar outlook for the president's popularity with Americans.

In a new Focaldata/Financial Times poll released over Labor Day weekend, the president hit a new record low, as only 32% of Americans said they approved of Trump's job performance. This performance was three percentage points worse than the same poll done in August.

According to Focaldata/Financial Times, Trump's 32% approval is also the worst the president has seen since the poll began tracking it in May.

Trump's approval with Republicans also slipped by 2 percentage points, down to 72%.

Only days before Grammer's prediction, Trump echoed a similar sentiment as he updated his ranking of U.S. presidents in a post on Truth Social.

The initial ranking appeared on Trump's Truth Social account Aug. 27 and listed the 80-year-old as "The Greatest," with Abraham Lincoln, George Washington, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Thomas Jefferson and Andrew Jackson on the next tier down, labeled "Great."

The newest ranking, posted Sept. 6, added several former presidents who were absent from the first list, including Ronald Reagan, John F. Kennedy, Gerald Ford and George W. Bush, among others. Reagan, long known as a conservative icon by many, was placed in the "Near Great" tier.

While individual polls vary, major polling averages continue to show Trump in negative territory overall:

RealClearPolitics (Sept. 9): 39.6% approve, 57.1% disapprove

New York Times (Sept. 9): 38% approve, 58% disapprove

Silver Bulletin (Sept. 9): 38.4% approve, 58% disapprove

USA TODAY's Gabe Hauari & KiMi Robinson contributed to this report.

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

title: Gavin Newsom expresses 'openness' to packing SCOTUS, calls Electoral College system 'perverted'
description: Dem California Gov. Gavin Newsom said he was "evolving" on the idea of expanding the Supreme Court and eliminating the Electoral College during an interview Tuesday.
fullText:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom expressed "openness" to reforming the Supreme Court and claimed the Electoral College "perverted" politics during an interview with former CNN host Don Lemon on his podcast Tuesday.

Near the end of the interview, Lemon directly asked Newsom, a rumored 2028 candidate, whether he believed the judicial branch needed to be expanded, an idea pushed by several Democratic figures, including former Vice President Kamala Harris.

"My initial instinct — me, a year ago, I would have said no out of concern that it will continue to be expanded," Newsom said.

"And I was making a case for the ethical reforms and term limits, 18 years, which I was making a case a year ago. I'm more open to it on the basis of those district court arguments, which are not terrible arguments."

Democratic Senator Claims Gop 'Stole' Two Scotus Seats In 2016, 2020, Calls For Expansion

"I'm finding myself evolving on it. I normally have very clear conviction on things. I've been open to argument and interested in the evidence on this," Newsom answered.

He described his position as "caution on expanding it, but openness," adding that he believes reforms like term limits are a "no-brainer."

Harris Labeled 'Institutional Arsonist' For Plan To Fundamentally Transform Scotus And Electoral College

The California Democrat had harsher criticism of the Electoral College, suggesting that it has "perverted" U.S. politics.

"California has already been a leader that's already gone out front saying it's time to change that system. Which state's more burdened by it than my state? We're the size of 21 state populations combined. Come on. And we have two representatives in the Senate? Come on.

"And the way that thing favors ... it's perverted, I think, our politics. The Constitution is a living document, and it was conceived to be amended, and I think it's time to make that amendment," Newsom said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment.

Carville Tells Dems To Quietly Prepare Power Grab With Dc, Puerto Rico Statehood And Supreme Court Packing

Though Newsom has not explicitly supported expanding the Supreme Court, he made similar comments suggesting an openness to it during an interview with Brian Tyler Cohen on his podcast in June. Cohen was arguing in favor of court expansion, and Newsom remarked that Cohen was "getting me closer to your point of view."

During an interview with "PBS NewsHour" on Monday, Newsom also said the Democratic Party is "pretty aligned" with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) on issues like universal healthcare, climate change and moving off fossil fuels. The DSA's goals include eliminating the Supreme Court and replacing it with a judiciary that would be selected by Congress.

House Democrats recently voted against a constitutional amendment to cap the number of justices on the Supreme Court at nine. Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Ariz., who introduced the measure, warned Congress about the downsides of expanding the court.

"Here's the question every American should ask: If a sitting majority can change the size of the Supreme Court the moment it dislikes rulings, what happens to the next time the other side is in power?" Biggs said on the floor.

title: Appeals Court Grants Immunity to Texas Cops Who Held Handcuffed Woman Face Down in a Fire Ant Hill
description: The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that Taylor Rogers didn't show that it was clearly established that it was excessive force to be held down on a pile of fire ants while handcuffed.
fullText:
A federal appeals court ruled that a Texas woman can't sue two Santa Fe police officers who pinned her face down on a fire ant hill while she was handcuffed, causing her to receive hundreds of painful bites to her face.

In an August 6 opinion, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit reversed a lower court decision allowing Taylor Rogers' lawsuit against the City of Santa Fe and the two officers to move forward. Instead, the panel held that the officers were shielded from her claims under the doctrine of qualified immunity.

In a press conference last Friday, Rogers' attorney, Randy Kallinen, criticized the ruling.

"The United States 5th Circuit Court of Appeals is out of touch with the Constitution and the public, granting police immunity in the most egregious of cases," Kallinen said. "The people need to elect officials who will nominate and affirm judges loyal to the Constitution."

Kallinen told The Daily News that he has requested an en banc hearing for the full 15-member 5th Circuit to review the case, and he'll petition the Supreme Court for review if that fails.

"The facts, injuries and footage speaks for itself," Kallinen said. "If they let this one slide, they're letting police do just about anything."

Santa Fe Independent School District Police officers arrested Rogers in 2021 after she drove erratically through a school parking lot and disobeyed commands to stop. According to the 5th Circuit opinion, she continued to thrash and resist officers in a state of hysteria after being handcuffed.

Santa Fe ISD officer Christian Carranza then threw Rogers to the ground and held her face down in a pile of fire ants while twisting her legs upward, effectively hog-tying her.

Body camera footage released by Kallinen showed Rogers begging for Carranza to stop while multiple other officers watched. "Ants are on my face! Ants are getting on my face, please!" Rogers yelled. "How can y'all do this? Ants are on my face! Please let go!"

After pleading guilty to felony evading arrest, Rogers filed a civil rights lawsuit in 2023 alleging excessive force, failure to intervene, cruel and unusual punishment, and deprivation of due process. Pictures accompanying Rogers' lawsuit showed her face, neck, and upper chest covered with hundreds of ant bites.

"No reasonable officer would have held Ms. Rogers legs up and behind her body whilst also pressing her face and torso into a pile of fire ants," Rogers' lawsuit said, noting that she is 5 feet, 7 inches tall and weighs roughly 130 pounds.

However, the officers argued they were entitled to qualified immunity, a legal doctrine that makes government officials immune from lawsuits when the constitutional right they are accused of violating isn't clearly established.

Last June, a federal judge allowed Rogers' lawsuit to proceed and ruled that the two Santa Fe officers weren't entitled to qualified immunity.

The 5th Circuit panel reversed that decision, ruling that because Rogers couldn't point to analogous case law finding that using a leg-leverage technique to restrain a resisting suspect on top of a fire ant hill was unconstitutional excessive force, her claims were barred by qualified immunity.

Civil liberties groups and criminal justice advocates have long argued that qualified immunity allows police officers to drag out lawsuits for years and stop cases from ever being considered by jury, even in cases of egregious abuse, such as detectives lying under oath or correctional officers who watched a jail inmate die soaked in his own vomit over the course of 13 hours.

The post Appeals Court Grants Immunity to Texas Cops Who Held Handcuffed Woman Face Down in a Fire Ant Hill appeared first on Reason Magazine.
